BMA-01.Planning: Deciding the goals of the business and the steps to reach them, before the work starts.
BMA-01.Organizing: Arranging people, tasks and resources so the plan can be carried out, including who does what and who reports to whom.
BMA-01.Leading: Guiding and inspiring employees so they work willingly toward the company's goals. Some textbooks call this function directing.
BMA-01.Controlling: Comparing actual results with the plan and correcting anything that is off track.
BMA-01.Implementing: Putting a plan into action. Some textbooks list it as a management function in place of leading.
BMA-01.Motivating: Giving employees reasons to work hard, such as recognition, rewards or interesting work. It is often treated as part of leading.
BMA-01.Staffing: Finding, hiring, training and keeping the right people for each job. Some frameworks count it as its own function.
BMA-01.Decision making: Choosing between alternatives. Managers do this within every other function, so some lists name it separately.
BMA-01.Commanding: Giving instructions to employees so the work gets done. It is one of the five functions in Henri Fayol's original list.
BMA-01.Coordinating: Making sure different people and departments work together and on the same timing. It is one of Henri Fayol's five functions.
BMA-01.Budgeting: Planning how money will be received and spent. It is the B in POSDCORB, an older list of what managers do.
BMA-01.Reporting: Keeping superiors and others informed through records and updates. It is the R in POSDCORB, an older list of management functions.

BMA-02.Democratic: The leader asks the team for ideas and opinions before deciding, so employees share in decisions. Also called participative leadership.
BMA-02.Autocratic: The leader makes decisions alone and expects employees to follow orders without much input.
BMA-02.Laissez-faire: A hands-off style in which the leader gives little direction and lets employees decide how to do their work. The French phrase means "let do".
BMA-02.Transformational: The leader inspires people with a vision of change and encourages them to grow and go beyond what they thought they could do.
BMA-02.Servant leadership: The leader puts the needs and growth of team members first, on the idea that well-supported people do the best work.
BMA-02.Transactional: The leader manages through a clear exchange: rewards for meeting targets and penalties for missing them.
BMA-02.Coaching: The leader acts like a coach, helping each employee build skills and reach long-term personal and career goals.
BMA-02.Visionary: The leader sets out a clear picture of where the organization is going and lets people find their own way to get there.
BMA-02.Affiliative: The leader focuses on harmony and good relationships, putting people's feelings and team bonds first.
BMA-02.Bureaucratic: The leader goes strictly by written rules, procedures and the chain of command, treating everyone by the book.
BMA-02.Charismatic: The leader wins followers through personal charm, energy and persuasive communication.
BMA-02.Paternalistic: The leader acts like a parent, making the decisions but looking after employees' welfare and expecting loyalty in return.
BMA-02.Situational: The leader changes style to fit the task and how ready the team is, directing new workers closely and delegating to experienced ones.
BMA-02.Pacesetting: The leader sets very high standards, shows them by personal example and expects the team to keep up.
BMA-02.Strategic: The leader keeps attention on long-term direction and competitive position while still handling day-to-day operations.
BMA-02.Authentic: The leader is open and honest about personal values and acts on them consistently, which builds trust.

BMA-03.Hierarchical: A pyramid-shaped structure with many levels of management, where authority flows down a clear chain of command from the top.
BMA-03.Flat: A structure with few or no levels of middle management, so employees are close to the top decision makers.
BMA-03.Functional: Employees are grouped into departments by the kind of work they do, such as marketing, finance and production.
BMA-03.Centralized: Decision-making power is kept by a small group of top managers, and lower levels carry the decisions out.
BMA-03.Decentralized: Decision-making power is pushed down to lower-level managers and local units, who can act without asking the top first.
BMA-03.Matrix: Employees report to two managers at once, usually a functional manager and a project or product manager.
BMA-03.Divisional: The company is split into semi-independent divisions, often one for each product line, each with its own staff for key functions.
BMA-03.Team-based: Work is organized around teams, often with members from different functions, which make many of their own decisions.
BMA-03.Geographic: The company is divided by region or territory, so each area has its own managers who know the local market.
BMA-03.Customer-based: Departments are built around types of customer, such as consumers, businesses and government buyers.
BMA-03.Project-based: People are grouped into temporary teams for each project and report to a project manager until it is finished.
BMA-03.Line and staff: Line managers have direct authority over the main work, while staff specialists such as legal or human resources advise and support them.
BMA-03.Network: A small central company contracts out most functions to other firms and coordinates them, instead of doing everything itself.
BMA-03.Process-based: The company is organized around its main work flows from start to finish, such as order fulfillment, instead of around departments.
BMA-03.Holacracy: A system without traditional managers, in which authority is spread across self-organizing teams called circles and people fill defined roles.
BMA-03.Circular: A structure drawn as rings, with top leaders at the center and each outer ring a lower level, meant to show information flowing outward.

ECO-01.Labor: The physical and mental work people put into producing goods and services. Its payment is wages.
ECO-01.Land: All natural resources used in production, such as soil, water, minerals, oil and timber, not just ground.
ECO-01.Capital: Human-made goods used to produce other goods and services, such as machines, tools and buildings.
ECO-01.Entrepreneurship: The willingness to take risks and combine land, labor and capital to start and run a business. Its reward is profit.
ECO-01.Human capital: The knowledge, skills and experience workers have. It makes labor more productive, and some texts treat it as a resource of its own.
ECO-01.Technology: The methods and know-how used to turn inputs into outputs. Some newer texts list it as a separate resource because it raises productivity.
ECO-01.Knowledge: Information and expertise used in production. Some newer textbooks add it as a fifth factor of production.

ECO-02.Monopoly: A market with only one seller of a product that has no close substitutes, which gives that seller strong control over price.
ECO-02.Oligopoly: A market dominated by a few large sellers, each of which watches and reacts to what the others do.
ECO-02.Perfect competition: A market with many small sellers of identical products and easy entry, so no single seller can influence the price.
ECO-02.Monopolistic competition: A market with many sellers whose products are similar but not identical, so they compete on brand, quality and features as well as price.
ECO-02.Natural monopoly: An industry where one firm can serve the whole market at a lower cost than two or more could, such as a local water system.
ECO-02.Duopoly: A market controlled by just two sellers. It is the smallest form of oligopoly.
ECO-02.Monopsony: A market with only one buyer and many sellers, which gives the buyer the power to push prices down.
ECO-02.Oligopsony: A market with only a few large buyers and many sellers, so the buyers have strong power over price.
ECO-02.Bilateral monopoly: A market with a single seller facing a single buyer, so the price depends on bargaining between the two.

ECO-03.Gross domestic product: The total market value of all final goods and services produced inside a country in a period, usually a year or a quarter. Known as GDP.
ECO-03.Unemployment rate: The percentage of people in the labor force who do not have a job and are actively looking for one.
ECO-03.Inflation rate: The percentage by which the general level of prices rises over a period, usually a year.
ECO-03.Interest rates: The cost of borrowing money, shown as a percentage of the loan. Low rates encourage borrowing and spending, and high rates slow them.
ECO-03.Consumer price index: A measure of the average change in prices paid by households for a fixed basket of goods and services. The CPI is the main gauge of inflation.
ECO-03.Stock market: Share prices, tracked by indexes such as the S&P 500, show how investors expect companies to perform. They tend to move ahead of the economy.
ECO-03.National debt: The total amount the federal government owes from borrowing to cover past budget deficits.
ECO-03.Consumer spending: The total households spend on goods and services. It makes up the largest share of the U.S. economy.
ECO-03.Gross national product: The total value of goods and services produced by a country's residents and businesses in a year, wherever in the world they operate. Known as GNP.
ECO-03.Consumer confidence: A survey-based measure of how optimistic households feel about the economy and their own finances, which hints at future spending.
ECO-03.Retail sales: The total sales of stores and online retailers in a period, reported monthly. It shows how strongly consumers are spending.
ECO-03.Trade balance: The difference between the value of a country's exports and its imports. A surplus means more exports, and a deficit means more imports.
ECO-03.Personal income: The income people receive from wages, investments and other sources. Rising income usually means more spending.
ECO-03.Housing starts: The number of new homes on which construction began in a period. It signals builder and buyer confidence and tends to lead the economy.
ECO-03.Producer price index: A measure of the average change in prices that producers receive for their output. The PPI can warn of consumer price changes to come.
ECO-03.Jobless claims: The number of people filing for unemployment insurance benefits, reported weekly. A rise suggests layoffs are increasing.
ECO-03.Productivity: The amount of output produced per hour of work. Rising productivity lets an economy grow and wages rise without higher prices.
ECO-03.Industrial production: A measure of the output of factories, mines and utilities. It shows how busy the goods-producing side of the economy is.
ECO-03.Jobs report: The monthly U.S. government report on how many jobs employers added or cut and on the unemployment rate.
ECO-03.Exchange rates: The price of one country's currency in terms of another's. They affect how costly imports and exports are.
ECO-03.Business investment: Spending by companies on equipment, buildings and technology. Firms invest more when they expect the economy to grow.
ECO-03.Durable goods orders: New orders placed with manufacturers for long-lasting items such as machinery, appliances and vehicles. They signal future factory activity.
ECO-03.Yield curve: A graph of interest rates on government bonds from short-term to long-term. When short-term rates rise above long-term ones, it often warns of a recession.
ECO-03.Purchasing managers index: A monthly survey of purchasing managers about orders, output and hiring. A PMI reading above 50 means the sector is expanding.
ECO-03.Labor force participation rate: The percentage of the working-age population that is either working or actively looking for work.
ECO-03.Money supply: The total amount of money in the economy, such as cash and bank deposits. M1 and M2 are the common measures.

BA-01.Marketing: The department that studies customers and promotes the company's products through advertising, branding and campaigns.
BA-01.Human resources: The department that recruits, hires and trains employees and handles pay, benefits and workplace policies. Often shortened to HR.
BA-01.Finance: The department that manages the company's money, including budgets, investments, borrowing and financial planning.
BA-01.Accounting: The department that records every financial transaction, pays bills and employees, and prepares the financial statements.
BA-01.Sales: The department whose staff deal directly with customers to close deals and bring in revenue.
BA-01.Operations: The department that makes the product or delivers the service, turning inputs into finished output efficiently.
BA-01.Information technology: The department that runs the company's computers, networks, software and data, and helps employees with technical problems. Known as IT.
BA-01.Customer service: The department that answers customer questions, solves problems and handles complaints after and around a sale.
BA-01.Management: The executives and administrators who set direction, make major decisions and oversee all the other departments.
BA-01.Research and development: The department that creates new products and improves existing ones through research and testing. Known as R&D.
BA-01.Legal: The company's lawyers, who review contracts, give legal advice and handle lawsuits and regulatory matters.
BA-01.Public relations: The department that manages the company's image and its communication with the media and the public. Known as PR.
BA-01.Engineering: The department that designs products and works out the technical details of how they will be built.
BA-01.Purchasing: The department that buys the materials, supplies and services the company needs, choosing suppliers and negotiating prices.
BA-01.Logistics: The department that plans how goods are stored and moved, from suppliers to the company and on to customers.
BA-01.Training and development: The department, often part of human resources, that teaches employees the skills they need now and for future roles.
BA-01.Security: The department that protects the company's people, buildings and property from theft and other threats.
BA-01.Facilities: The department that looks after the company's buildings and grounds, including maintenance, repairs and cleaning.
BA-01.Quality assurance: The department that checks processes and products to make sure they meet the required standard before reaching customers.
BA-01.Compliance: The department that makes sure the company and its employees follow the laws, regulations and internal rules that apply to them.
BA-01.Internal audit: A team inside the company that independently checks financial records and controls to find errors, waste or fraud.
BA-01.Investor relations: The department that communicates with shareholders and financial analysts about the company's performance and plans.
BA-01.Risk management: The department that identifies what could harm the company, such as accidents or lawsuits, and plans how to reduce or insure against it.

BA-02.Customers: The people and organizations that buy the company's products. They are affected by its prices, quality and safety.
BA-02.Employees: The people who work for the business. Their pay, job security and working conditions depend on how it performs.
BA-02.Owners: The people who have invested money in the business, including shareholders of a corporation. They gain or lose as profits rise or fall.
BA-02.Managers: The people who run the business. Their careers, pay and reputations are tied to its success.
BA-02.Suppliers: The businesses that sell materials, goods or services to the company. They depend on its orders and on being paid on time.
BA-02.Community: The people who live near the business. It affects them through jobs, traffic, pollution and support for local causes.
BA-02.Government: Public bodies that collect taxes from the business and set and enforce the laws and regulations it must follow.
BA-02.Distributors: Wholesalers, retailers and other intermediaries that resell the company's products and rely on them for their own sales.
BA-02.Creditors: Banks and others that have lent the business money and want to be repaid with interest.
BA-02.Competitors: Rival businesses selling to the same customers. Some texts count them as stakeholders because the company's actions affect their sales and prices.
BA-02.Business partners: Other companies that work closely with the business, such as franchisees or joint venture partners, and share in its results.
BA-02.Environment: The natural world, which is affected by the resources a business uses and the waste and pollution it creates.
BA-02.Labor unions: Organizations that represent workers and bargain with the company over pay, hours and working conditions.
BA-02.Media: News organizations that report on the business and shape how the public sees it.
BA-02.Advocacy groups: Organizations that campaign on issues such as the environment or consumer rights and press businesses to change their behavior.
BA-02.Trade associations: Organizations of businesses in the same industry that set standards, share information and speak for their members.

BA-03.Job postings: Advertisements for an open position placed on job websites, in newspapers or on signs so that people can apply.
BA-03.Interviews: Meetings in which an employer asks a candidate questions to judge skills, experience and fit for the job.
BA-03.Employee referrals: Current employees recommend people they know for open jobs. Some companies pay a reward when a referred person is hired.
BA-03.Resume screening: Reviewing resumes and application forms to pick out the candidates who meet the job's requirements, sometimes with tracking software.
BA-03.Social media: Using sites such as LinkedIn to advertise openings and to search for and contact possible candidates.
BA-03.Company website: A careers page on the employer's own site where openings are listed and people can apply directly.
BA-03.Job fairs: Events where many employers set up booths to meet job seekers, collect resumes and sometimes interview on the spot.
BA-03.Staffing agencies: Outside firms that find candidates for an employer for a fee. Some supply temporary workers, and some search for executives.
BA-03.Internships: Short-term work placements for students. They let the employer try out possible future hires while the student gains experience.
BA-03.Background checks: Checking a candidate's history, such as criminal record, past jobs and education, before making a final hiring decision.
BA-03.Skills tests: Tests that measure whether a candidate has the abilities or knowledge the job needs, such as typing, math or software skills.
BA-03.Phone screening: A short phone or video call used early in the process to decide which applicants should be invited to a full interview.
BA-03.Campus recruiting: Visiting colleges and working with their career centers to find and hire students and recent graduates.
BA-03.Internal promotion: Filling an opening with a current employee, by promotion or transfer, instead of hiring from outside.
BA-03.Reference checks: Contacting a candidate's former employers or teachers to confirm what the candidate has said and learn how they performed.
BA-03.Drug testing: Testing a candidate for illegal drug use as a condition of being hired, common in safety-sensitive jobs.
BA-03.Personality tests: Questionnaires that measure traits such as honesty, teamwork or attention to detail to predict how a candidate will behave at work.
BA-03.Group interviews: Interviews in which several candidates are seen together, or one candidate faces a panel of several interviewers.
BA-03.Assessment centers: A selection method in which candidates spend a day or more on simulated work exercises while trained assessors watch and score them.
BA-03.Work samples: Asking candidates to perform a real piece of the job, or show a portfolio of past work, so the employer can judge actual ability.
BA-03.Structured interviews: Interviews in which every candidate is asked the same planned questions and scored the same way, which makes comparison fairer.
BA-03.Rehiring former employees: Bringing back people who used to work for the company. They already know the business and need less training.
BA-03.State employment agencies: Government-run offices that list job openings and match unemployed workers with employers at no charge.

POB-01.Time utility: Value added by having a product available when customers want it, such as a store that is open late or stocks seasonal goods in season.
POB-01.Place utility: Value added by having a product available where customers want it, such as in a nearby store or delivered to the door.
POB-01.Form utility: Value added by changing materials into a more useful product, such as turning wood into a chair.
POB-01.Possession utility: Value added by making it easy for the customer to take ownership, for example by accepting credit cards or offering payment plans.
POB-01.Information utility: Value added by telling customers about a product, through advertising, labels, salespeople or instructions.
POB-01.Task utility: Value added when someone performs a service for the customer, such as a mechanic repairing a car. Only some texts list it.

POB-02.Selling: Finding out what customers need and helping them choose and buy a product through direct, personal contact.
POB-02.Promotion: Communicating with customers to inform, persuade or remind them about products, through advertising, publicity and sales promotions.
POB-02.Pricing: Deciding how much to charge so that customers see good value and the business still makes a profit.
POB-02.Product/service management: Developing, improving and maintaining the mix of goods and services a business offers in response to what the market wants.
POB-02.Channel management: Deciding how products get from the producer to the customer, including which intermediaries, transport and storage to use. Also called distribution.
POB-02.Financing: Getting the money needed to pay for marketing activities and helping customers pay, for example by offering credit. Listed in older versions of the functions.
POB-02.Marketing-information management: Gathering, storing and analyzing information about customers, competitors and trends so that marketing decisions are based on facts.
POB-02.Market planning: Understanding the market and choosing which customers to target and what strategies to use to reach them.
POB-02.Buying: Obtaining the goods a business needs to resell or use. It appears in a traditional older list of eight marketing functions.
POB-02.Risk taking: Accepting the chance of loss that comes with owning and marketing goods, such as damage, theft or poor sales. Named in older lists of the functions.
POB-02.Standardizing and grading: Setting uniform specifications for products and sorting them by quality, so buyers know what they are getting. Named in older lists of the functions.

POB-03.Transfer it with insurance: Paying a premium to an insurance company, which then agrees to cover the financial loss if the insured event happens.
POB-03.Avoid it: Choosing not to do the risky activity at all, such as refusing to sell a product that could easily injure someone.
POB-03.Reduce it: Taking steps that make a loss less likely or less severe, such as safety training, sprinklers and security systems.
POB-03.Retain it: Accepting the risk and paying for any loss out of the business's own money, often from a fund set aside for the purpose.
POB-03.Diversify: Spreading activity across several products, markets or investments so that a loss in one does not sink the whole business.
POB-03.Share it: Dividing a risk with others, for example by taking on a partner or forming a joint venture, so no one party bears the full loss.
POB-03.Outsource it: Using a contract to pass a risky activity, and responsibility for it, to another company that specializes in that work.
POB-03.Contingency planning: Preparing a backup plan in advance so the business can keep running if something goes wrong, such as a fire or a data loss.
POB-03.Hedge: Taking a financial position that gains when another loses, such as a futures contract that locks in the price of fuel or a crop.
POB-03.Incorporate for limited liability: Forming a corporation or limited liability company so that owners can lose only what they invested, not their personal assets.

LAW-01.Offer: A clear proposal by one party to enter into an agreement on definite terms, which the other party can accept or reject.
LAW-01.Acceptance: The other party's clear agreement to the exact terms of the offer. Changing the terms makes it a counteroffer instead.
LAW-01.Consideration: Something of value that each side gives or promises to the other, such as money, goods or a service. Without it, a promise is only a gift.
LAW-01.Capacity: The legal ability to enter into a contract. Minors and people who are mentally incompetent generally lack full capacity.
LAW-01.Legality: The purpose of the contract must be lawful. Courts will not enforce an agreement to do something illegal.
LAW-01.Genuine assent: Both parties must truly and freely agree to the same terms. Fraud, duress or a serious mistake means the agreement was not genuine.
LAW-01.Proper form: Some contracts, such as those for the sale of land, must be in writing and signed to be enforced, under a rule called the statute of frauds.
LAW-01.Intention to create legal relations: Both parties must mean the agreement to be legally binding. A casual social promise, such as meeting for lunch, is not a contract.

LAW-02.Copyright: Legal protection for original creative works such as books, music, films and software, giving the creator the right to control copying and use.
LAW-02.Patent: A government grant giving an inventor the exclusive right to make, use and sell an invention for a limited time, generally 20 years.
LAW-02.Trademark: Legal protection for a word, name, symbol or logo that identifies a company's goods and sets them apart from competitors'.
LAW-02.Trade secret: Valuable business information, such as a formula or recipe, that is protected by law as long as the owner takes reasonable steps to keep it secret.
LAW-02.Non-disclosure agreement: A contract in which a person promises not to reveal confidential information. Businesses use it to help keep trade secrets protected.
LAW-02.Service mark: The same kind of protection as a trademark, but for a name or symbol that identifies a service instead of a physical product.
LAW-02.Design patent: A patent that protects the new, original ornamental appearance of a manufactured item, not the way it works.
LAW-02.Plant patent: A patent for someone who invents or discovers a new variety of plant and reproduces it asexually, for example by cuttings or grafting.
LAW-02.Trade dress: Protection for the distinctive overall look of a product or its packaging, such as shape and color scheme, that tells buyers who makes it.
LAW-02.Geographical indication: A protected name for a product that comes from a particular place and owes its qualities or reputation to it, such as Champagne.
LAW-02.Industrial design right: Protection, used in many countries, for the visual design of an object, such as its shape, pattern or color.
LAW-02.Certification mark: A mark showing that goods or services meet a standard set by the mark's owner, such as a safety or origin standard. Others who qualify may use it.

LAW-03.FDA: The Food and Drug Administration. It regulates the safety of most foods, medicines, medical devices and cosmetics.
LAW-03.IRS: The Internal Revenue Service. It collects federal taxes and enforces the tax laws that businesses and individuals must follow.
LAW-03.FTC: The Federal Trade Commission. It protects consumers from deceptive advertising and unfair business practices and helps enforce antitrust law.
LAW-03.EPA: The Environmental Protection Agency. It sets and enforces rules on pollution of air, water and land.
LAW-03.SEC: The Securities and Exchange Commission. It regulates the stock markets and requires public companies to give investors honest information.
LAW-03.OSHA: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration. It sets workplace safety standards and inspects employers to enforce them.
LAW-03.FCC: The Federal Communications Commission. It regulates radio, television, telephone, cable and satellite communication.
LAW-03.USDA: The U.S. Department of Agriculture. It inspects meat, poultry and egg products, grades farm goods and oversees farming programs.
LAW-03.EEOC: The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. It enforces federal laws against discrimination in hiring, pay and other job decisions.
LAW-03.Department of Labor: The federal department that enforces laws on wages, overtime, child labor and other working conditions.
LAW-03.FAA: The Federal Aviation Administration. It regulates airlines, pilots, aircraft and airports to keep air travel safe.
LAW-03.Federal Reserve: The central bank of the United States. It sets monetary policy and supervises and regulates many banks.
LAW-03.Department of Justice: The federal department that enforces federal law. Its Antitrust Division challenges monopolies, price fixing and anticompetitive mergers.
LAW-03.Department of Transportation: The federal department that sets safety rules for highways, railroads, airlines, pipelines and other transport.
LAW-03.Department of Commerce: The federal department that promotes economic growth and trade. It also controls certain exports and gathers business and census data.
LAW-03.CPSC: The Consumer Product Safety Commission. It sets safety standards for consumer products and can order recalls of dangerous ones.
LAW-03.CFPB: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. It regulates consumer financial products such as mortgages, credit cards and loans.
LAW-03.FDIC: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. It insures bank deposits and supervises many banks for safety and soundness.
LAW-03.Patent and Trademark Office: The federal agency that examines applications and grants patents and registers trademarks.
LAW-03.Department of the Treasury: The federal department that manages the government's money and debt. It includes the Internal Revenue Service and enforces economic sanctions.
LAW-03.Customs and Border Protection: The agency that inspects goods entering the country, collects import duties and enforces trade laws at the border.
LAW-03.NHTSA: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. It sets vehicle safety standards and oversees recalls of unsafe cars.
LAW-03.ATF: The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. It licenses and regulates businesses that make or sell firearms and explosives.
LAW-03.NLRB: The National Labor Relations Board. It runs union elections and rules on unfair labor practice complaints against employers and unions.
LAW-03.CFTC: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission. It regulates the markets where futures and other derivatives contracts are traded.
LAW-03.FERC: The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. It regulates the interstate transmission of electricity, natural gas and oil.
LAW-03.OCC: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency. It charters, regulates and supervises national banks.
LAW-03.FMCSA: The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. It sets safety rules for trucking and bus companies and their drivers.
LAW-03.Nuclear Regulatory Commission: The agency that licenses and regulates nuclear power plants and the civilian use of radioactive materials.
LAW-03.TTB: The Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau. It collects federal taxes on alcohol and tobacco and regulates their production and labeling.
LAW-03.Surface Transportation Board: The agency that regulates the economics of freight railroads, including rates, service disputes and rail mergers.
LAW-03.Federal Maritime Commission: The agency that regulates international ocean shipping to and from the United States to keep it fair and competitive.

HRM-01.Health insurance: A plan that pays much of the cost of doctor visits, hospital stays and medicines. The employer usually pays part of the premium.
HRM-01.Paid time off: Days an employee can take away from work, for vacation or personal reasons, while still being paid. Often shortened to PTO.
HRM-01.Retirement plan: A plan that helps employees save for retirement, such as a 401(k) to which the employer may add matching money, or a pension.
HRM-01.Sick leave: Paid days off that an employee can use when ill or injured, without losing wages.
HRM-01.Dental or vision insurance: Dental insurance helps pay for checkups, fillings and other tooth care. Vision insurance helps pay for eye exams, glasses and contact lenses.
HRM-01.Life insurance: A policy, often paid for by the employer, that pays money to the employee's family if the employee dies.
HRM-01.Employee discounts: Reduced prices for employees on the company's own products or services.
HRM-01.Paid holidays: Public holidays, such as Thanksgiving, on which employees get the day off and are still paid.
HRM-01.Parental leave: Time off for a new mother or father after a birth or adoption. Some employers pay for it, which federal law does not require.
HRM-01.Tuition reimbursement: The employer pays back some or all of the cost of college courses or other schooling that an employee completes.
HRM-01.Flexible work arrangements: Options that let employees change when or where they work, such as flexible start times, compressed weeks or working from home.
HRM-01.Stock options: The right to buy shares of the company's stock at a set price in the future, which becomes valuable if the share price rises.
HRM-01.Bonuses or profit sharing: A bonus is extra money paid for good results or at special times. Profit sharing pays employees a portion of the company's profits.
HRM-01.Child care assistance: Help with the cost or availability of child care, such as an on-site daycare center or money toward daycare fees.
HRM-01.Company car or equipment: A vehicle, phone or laptop that the employer provides and pays for, which the employee uses for work and sometimes personally.
HRM-01.Free meals: Food and drink provided by the employer at no cost, such as lunches, snacks or a subsidized cafeteria.
HRM-01.Disability insurance: Insurance that replaces part of an employee's income if an illness or injury leaves the employee unable to work.
HRM-01.Health or flexible spending account: Accounts that let employees set aside pre-tax money for medical costs. A health savings account rolls over each year. A flexible spending account mostly must be spent within the year.
HRM-01.Professional development: Training, courses, conferences and certifications paid for by the employer to help employees build career skills.
HRM-01.Commuter benefits: Help with the cost of getting to work, such as transit passes, free parking or a transportation allowance.
HRM-01.Relocation assistance: Money or services from the employer to cover the cost of moving when an employee takes a job in another city.
HRM-01.Bereavement or personal leave: Bereavement leave is paid time off after a death in the family. Personal leave is time off for private matters without giving a reason.
HRM-01.Workers compensation: Insurance paid for by the employer that covers medical bills and lost wages when an employee is hurt on the job. Most states require it.
HRM-01.Wellness program: Employer-sponsored activities that encourage healthy living, such as gym memberships, health screenings and fitness challenges.
HRM-01.Employee assistance program: A confidential service that gives employees free short-term counseling and referrals for personal problems such as stress or addiction.
HRM-01.Sabbatical: A long period of leave, often several weeks or months, given after years of service for rest, travel or study.
HRM-01.Student loan repayment: The employer makes payments toward an employee's existing student loans.
HRM-01.Adoption or fertility assistance: Adoption assistance helps pay the legal and agency costs of adopting a child. Fertility assistance helps pay for treatments to have a child.
HRM-01.Pet insurance: A plan offered through the employer that helps pay veterinary bills for an employee's pets.
HRM-01.Severance pay: Money paid to an employee who is laid off, often based on years of service, to help while the person looks for a new job.
HRM-01.Legal assistance plan: A plan that gives employees access to lawyers at low or no cost for personal matters such as wills or buying a home.

HRM-02.On-the-job training: Learning a job by doing it at the real workplace, under the guidance of a supervisor or experienced coworker.
HRM-02.Orientation: An introduction for new hires to the company's policies, culture, workplace and coworkers during their first days.
HRM-02.Job shadowing: A trainee follows and watches an experienced employee through the working day to see how the job is done.
HRM-02.Mentoring: An experienced employee is paired with a newer one to give advice, answer questions and guide career growth over time.
HRM-02.Online training: Courses, videos and quizzes delivered by computer or over the internet, which employees can often complete at their own pace.
HRM-02.Classroom training: An instructor teaches a group of employees away from their regular work, through lectures, workshops or seminars.
HRM-02.Training videos: Recorded video lessons that show employees a procedure or policy, so every viewer gets the same message.
HRM-02.Apprenticeship: A long program that combines paid on-the-job training under a skilled worker with classroom instruction, common in skilled trades.
HRM-02.Demonstration: A trainer shows step by step how to do a task, and the trainee then tries it.
HRM-02.Role-playing: Trainees act out a realistic work situation, such as handling an angry customer, to practice how they would respond.
HRM-02.Coaching: A supervisor or trainer works one on one with an employee, giving regular feedback and tips to improve performance.
HRM-02.Job rotation: Moving an employee through several different jobs for set periods to build a wider range of skills.
HRM-02.Internship: A temporary position, usually for a student, that gives supervised work experience in a career field.
HRM-02.Training manuals: Written guides, handbooks and step-by-step instructions that employees read and keep for reference.
HRM-02.Continuing education: Courses taken at a college or through a professional body to keep skills current or earn a certification, often with employer support.
HRM-02.Simulation: Practice on equipment or software that imitates real working conditions, such as a flight simulator, so mistakes cause no harm.
HRM-02.Case studies: Trainees read a detailed account of a real or made-up business situation, then analyze the problem and propose solutions.
HRM-02.Team-building exercises: Group activities and games designed to improve trust, communication and cooperation among coworkers.
HRM-02.Programmed instruction: Self-paced learning in which material is given in small steps, and the learner must answer a question correctly before moving on.
HRM-02.Vestibule training: Training in a separate practice area set up with the same equipment as the real workplace, so learners do not slow down actual work.
HRM-02.Microlearning: Training broken into very short lessons, often a few minutes each, that each cover one small topic.
HRM-02.Understudy assignment: An employee works closely under a senior person in order to learn that person's job and be ready to take it over.
HRM-02.Sensitivity training: Group sessions meant to make people more aware of their own behavior and biases and of how they affect others.
HRM-02.Job instruction training: A four-step on-the-job method: prepare the learner, show the task, have the learner try it, then follow up.

HRM-03.Race: A person's racial group. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 bars employers from basing job decisions on it.
HRM-03.Sex: Whether a person is male or female. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act bars job decisions based on it, and the Equal Pay Act requires equal pay for equal work.
HRM-03.Religion: A person's religious beliefs and practices. Employers may not discriminate because of them and must reasonably accommodate them.
HRM-03.Age: Being 40 or older. The Age Discrimination in Employment Act protects these workers from being treated worse because of their age.
HRM-03.Disability: A physical or mental impairment that substantially limits a major life activity. The Americans with Disabilities Act protects qualified workers who have one.
HRM-03.National origin: The country a person or the person's ancestors came from, including ethnicity and accent. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act protects it.
HRM-03.Color: The shade of a person's skin. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act lists it separately from race.
HRM-03.Pregnancy: Being pregnant, giving birth or having a related medical condition. The Pregnancy Discrimination Act of 1978 treats bias on this basis as sex discrimination.
HRM-03.Sexual orientation: Whether a person is gay, straight or bisexual. In 2020 the Supreme Court ruled that Title VII's ban on sex discrimination covers it.
HRM-03.Gender identity: A person's own sense of gender, including being transgender. In 2020 the Supreme Court ruled that Title VII's ban on sex discrimination covers it.
HRM-03.Veteran status: Past or present service in the armed forces. A federal law known as USERRA bars employers from penalizing people for military service.
HRM-03.Genetic information: Results of genetic tests and family medical history. A 2008 law bars employers from using this information in job decisions.
HRM-03.Citizenship status: Whether a person is a U.S. citizen or another kind of legally authorized worker. Federal immigration law bars most employers from discriminating on this basis.

HRM-04.Supervisor evaluation: The employee's direct manager rates the employee's work, usually in a formal review held once or twice a year.
HRM-04.Self-evaluation: Employees rate their own performance, listing achievements and areas to improve, usually before meeting with the manager.
HRM-04.360-degree feedback: Feedback is collected from everyone around the employee, including the manager, coworkers, subordinates and sometimes customers.
HRM-04.Peer review: Coworkers at the same level rate one another's work, since they see day-to-day performance up close.
HRM-04.Rating scale: The evaluator scores the employee on a list of traits or duties, such as quality of work, using a scale such as 1 to 5.
HRM-04.Management by objectives: Manager and employee agree on specific goals for a period, and the employee is then judged on how well those goals were met.
HRM-04.Productivity measures: Counting measurable results, such as units produced, sales made or calls handled, and comparing them with a target.
HRM-04.Direct observation: A supervisor watches the employee at work and judges performance from what is seen.
HRM-04.Customer feedback: Using customers' surveys, ratings and comments to judge how well an employee served them.
HRM-04.Checklist: The evaluator goes through a list of statements about job behavior and ticks the ones that describe the employee.
HRM-04.Ranking: The evaluator puts employees in order from best to worst, comparing them with one another instead of with a standard.
HRM-04.Regular check-ins: Frequent short meetings between manager and employee that give ongoing feedback, instead of waiting for an annual review.
HRM-04.Skills testing: Having employees take a test or perform a task to show they have the knowledge and skills the job requires.
HRM-04.Forced distribution: Managers must place set percentages of employees in each rating category, such as the top 20 percent and the bottom 10 percent.
HRM-04.Critical incident method: The supervisor keeps a written record of specific examples of especially good or poor behavior and uses them in the review.
HRM-04.Upward feedback: Employees rate their own manager, usually anonymously, on how well he or she leads and supports them.
HRM-04.Attendance records: Records of absences and late arrivals, used as a measure of how reliable an employee is.
HRM-04.Mystery shoppers: People hired to pose as ordinary customers and report on the service they received from employees.
HRM-04.Behaviorally anchored rating scale: A rating scale on which each score is tied to a written example of the specific behavior that earns it. Often shortened to BARS.
HRM-04.Essay method: The evaluator writes a description of the employee's strengths, weaknesses and potential in his or her own words.
HRM-04.Behavioral observation scale: The evaluator rates how often the employee shows each of a list of specific job behaviors, from almost never to almost always.
HRM-04.Assessment center: Employees complete simulated work exercises while trained observers score them, often to judge readiness for promotion.
HRM-04.Objectives and key results: A goal system in which each objective is paired with a few measurable results that show progress toward it. Known as OKRs.

OPM-01.Security cameras: Video cameras that record activity in the store. They deter thieves who know they are being watched and provide evidence afterward.
OPM-01.Security guards: Uniformed or plainclothes staff who watch for theft, deter shoplifters by their presence and may detain suspects.
OPM-01.Alarm system: Sensors on doors, windows or in rooms that sound an alert when someone breaks in or opens something they should not.
OPM-01.Security tags: Tags attached to merchandise that set off an alarm at the exit unless a cashier removes or deactivates them at checkout.
OPM-01.Locked display cases: Cabinets or locked hooks for costly or often-stolen items, so a customer must ask an employee to get the product.
OPM-01.Greeting customers: Staff acknowledge each shopper who comes in. Shoplifters avoid stores where they have been noticed, so friendly attention deters them.
OPM-01.Employee training: Teaching staff how to spot suspicious behavior, what to do when they see it and how to follow store security rules.
OPM-01.Mirrors: Curved mirrors mounted in corners or on ceilings that let staff see into aisles and blind spots.
OPM-01.Good lighting: A brightly lit store and parking lot leave no dark corners for hiding merchandise and make thieves easier to see.
OPM-01.Receipt checks: An employee at the exit compares each shopper's receipt with the goods being carried out.
OPM-01.Fitting room limits: A cap on how many items a shopper can take into a fitting room, often with an attendant counting them in and out.
OPM-01.Warning signs: Posted notices, such as "Shoplifters will be prosecuted" or "Smile, you are on camera", that remind people they could be caught.
OPM-01.Inventory counts: Regularly counting stock and comparing it with the records to find out what is missing, where and how fast.
OPM-01.Background checks: Checking the history of job applicants before hiring, to avoid employing people with a record of theft or dishonesty.
OPM-01.Cash handling procedures: Rules for how money is counted, stored and deposited, such as counting each cash drawer at the end of a shift, so missing cash is noticed.
OPM-01.Bag restrictions: A rule that shoppers may not bring backpacks or large bags into the store, since they can be used to hide stolen goods.
OPM-01.Prosecuting shoplifters: A policy of calling the police and pressing charges against everyone caught stealing, which discourages others from trying.
OPM-01.Self-checkout monitoring: Attendants or cameras watching the self-checkout area to catch items that are not scanned or are scanned as something cheaper.
OPM-01.Limiting entrances and exits: Using few doors, placed where staff can watch them, so that nobody can leave unseen with unpaid goods.
OPM-01.Store layout: Arranging the store with low shelves, clear sight lines and registers near the exit so staff can see shoppers everywhere.
OPM-01.Safe: A strong locked box where cash is kept. Moving money from the registers into it limits how much a robber or dishonest employee can take.
OPM-01.Employee bag checks: Inspecting employees' bags and packages as they leave work, to discourage staff from walking out with merchandise.
OPM-01.Point-of-sale monitoring: Reviewing register data for unusual patterns, such as many voids, refunds or discounts by one cashier, that can signal employee theft.
OPM-01.Anonymous tip line: A phone number or website where employees can report theft by coworkers without giving their names.
OPM-01.Key control: Limiting who holds keys and codes for stockrooms, cases and the building, and keeping a record of who has them.
OPM-01.Display dummies: Putting empty boxes or a single shoe on the shelf while the real product is kept in the back until it is paid for.

OPM-02.Mass production: Making very large quantities of identical products, usually on an assembly line, which keeps the cost of each unit low.
OPM-02.Custom production: Making a product one at a time to a single customer's specifications. Also called job production.
OPM-02.Automation: Using machines, robots and computers to do production work with little human labor.
OPM-02.Batch production: Making a set quantity of one product, then switching the same equipment to make a batch of a different product.
OPM-02.Lean manufacturing: An approach that works to remove every kind of waste, such as extra inventory, waiting and defects, from the production process.
OPM-02.Just-in-time production: Making goods only as they are needed, with materials arriving right before use, so very little inventory is held.
OPM-02.Continuous production: Running a process nonstop, often around the clock, to make a steady flow of one product such as gasoline, steel or paper.
OPM-02.Outsourcing: Paying another company to make the product or some of its parts instead of making them in the firm's own factory.
OPM-02.Division of labor: Breaking production into small separate tasks, with each worker specializing in one, so the work is done faster.
OPM-02.Intermittent production: Production that starts and stops, with equipment reset between runs to make different products in smaller quantities.
OPM-02.Mass customization: Using flexible technology to make products tailored to each customer's choices at a cost close to that of mass production.
OPM-02.3D printing: Building an object layer by layer from a digital design. Also called additive manufacturing, it suits prototypes and small runs.
OPM-02.Computer-aided manufacturing: Using computer software to control machine tools and other production equipment, often working directly from a digital design.
OPM-02.Make to stock: Producing goods ahead of time based on forecast demand and keeping them in inventory until customers order.
OPM-02.Project production: Making one large, unique product, such as a bridge, ship or building, as a project with its own plan and team.
OPM-02.Standardization: Making products and parts to the same specifications every time, so parts are interchangeable and production is simpler.
OPM-02.Flexible manufacturing: A system of computer-controlled machines that can switch quickly between making different products with little downtime.
OPM-02.Cellular manufacturing: Arranging machines and workers into small groups, or cells, that each make a family of similar parts from start to finish.
OPM-02.Agile manufacturing: An approach built to respond very quickly to changes in what customers want, using flexible equipment, workers and suppliers.
OPM-02.Assemble to order: Keeping parts and subassemblies in stock and putting the final product together only after a customer orders it.
OPM-02.Smart manufacturing: Factories in which connected machines and sensors share data so production can be monitored and adjusted automatically. Also called Industry 4.0.
OPM-02.Modular production: Building a product from standard sections, or modules, that are made separately and then joined together.
OPM-02.Discrete manufacturing: Making distinct items that can be counted, such as cars, phones or furniture, as opposed to flowing goods such as oil or chemicals.

OPM-03.Quality control inspection: Checking or testing products, or a sample of them, to find the ones that do not meet the standard before they reach customers.
OPM-03.Total quality management: A company-wide philosophy in which every employee and every department is responsible for continually improving quality for the customer. Known as TQM.
OPM-03.Six Sigma: A data-driven method for cutting variation in a process, with the goal of no more than 3.4 defects per million opportunities.
OPM-03.Continuous improvement: Making many small, ongoing improvements to processes instead of waiting for one big change. The Japanese term is kaizen.
OPM-03.ISO 9000 standards: A family of international standards for quality management systems, published by the International Organization for Standardization. Companies can be certified to ISO 9001.
OPM-03.Customer feedback: Collecting surveys, reviews and complaints to learn where customers think quality falls short.
OPM-03.Quality standards: Written specifications and procedures that define exactly what an acceptable product or service looks like.
OPM-03.Employee training: Teaching workers the right way to do each task and how to spot problems, so fewer mistakes are made in the first place.
OPM-03.Benchmarking: Comparing the company's processes and results with those of the best performers and using them as the target to reach.
OPM-03.Quality circles: Small groups of employees who meet regularly to find and solve quality problems in their own work area.
OPM-03.Lean: An approach that improves quality and efficiency by removing waste, meaning any step that does not add value for the customer.
OPM-03.Quality audits: Systematic reviews of whether processes are being followed and whether the quality system is working as intended.
OPM-03.Checklists: Lists of the steps or items to verify, so that nothing is skipped. A check sheet is a similar form used to tally defects.
OPM-03.Statistical process control: Using statistics and control charts to watch a process as it runs and catch when it drifts outside normal limits.
OPM-03.PDCA cycle: Plan, Do, Check, Act: a repeating four-step loop for testing a change, studying the result and then adopting or adjusting it.
OPM-03.Root cause analysis: Digging past the symptoms of a problem to find its underlying cause, for example by asking "why" five times.
OPM-03.Malcolm Baldrige criteria: A U.S. framework for judging an organization's overall performance and quality, used for the Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award.
OPM-03.Supplier quality management: Checking and working with suppliers so that the materials and parts they deliver meet the buyer's standards.
OPM-03.Flowchart: A diagram of each step in a process in order, used to spot delays, repeated work and places where errors can occur.
OPM-03.Fishbone diagram: A chart shaped like a fish skeleton that sorts the possible causes of a problem into categories. Also called an Ishikawa diagram.
OPM-03.Pareto chart: A bar chart that ranks causes of problems from most to least frequent, showing the few causes that create most of the trouble.
OPM-03.Poka-yoke: A Japanese term for mistake-proofing: designing a process or part so that an error cannot be made or is obvious at once.
OPM-03.Zero defects: A program that sets the goal of doing the work right the first time, treating any defect as unacceptable instead of normal.
OPM-03.Failure mode and effects analysis: A step-by-step review of every way a product or process could fail and how serious each failure would be, done so the worst risks are fixed first.
OPM-03.Histogram: A bar graph showing how often each range of measurements occurs, which reveals how much a process varies.
OPM-03.Scatter diagram: A graph that plots two variables against each other to show whether they are related, such as temperature and defect rate.
OPM-03.5S: A workplace organization method with five steps: sort, set in order, shine, standardize and sustain.
OPM-03.Quality function deployment: A method for turning what customers say they want into specific design and production requirements, using a chart called the house of quality.

OPM-04.Barcode scanning: Reading the printed code on each item with a scanner so that stock received and sold is recorded quickly and accurately.
OPM-04.Physical inventory count: Counting by hand every item actually on the shelves and in storage, then comparing the totals with the records.
OPM-04.Inventory management software: A computer program that records what is in stock, what has been sold and what needs reordering, often linked to the checkout system.
OPM-04.Spreadsheet: A table, in a program such as Excel, where a small business lists each item and updates the quantities by hand.
OPM-04.Just-in-time inventory: Ordering stock so that it arrives only as it is needed, which keeps very little on hand and cuts storage costs.
OPM-04.Perpetual inventory system: A system that updates the inventory records with every sale and delivery, so the stock level is known at any moment.
OPM-04.First in, first out: Selling or using the oldest stock first so that goods do not expire or go out of date. Known as FIFO, it is also an accounting method for valuing inventory.
OPM-04.Last in, first out: Treating the newest stock as the first sold. Known as LIFO, it is mainly an accounting method for valuing inventory and the cost of goods sold.
OPM-04.Reorder point: The stock level at which a new order must be placed so that the delivery arrives before the item runs out.
OPM-04.Safety stock: Extra inventory kept on hand as a cushion against a sudden jump in demand or a late delivery.
OPM-04.RFID tags: Radio frequency identification tags: small chips on items or pallets that can be read by radio without being seen, so stock is tracked automatically.
OPM-04.Demand forecasting: Using past sales and trends to predict how much customers will buy, so the right amount of stock can be ordered.
OPM-04.Inventory turnover ratio: The number of times inventory is sold and replaced in a period. A high figure means stock moves quickly, and a low one means it sits.
OPM-04.Economic order quantity: A formula for the order size that makes the combined cost of placing orders and holding stock as low as possible. Known as EOQ.
OPM-04.ABC analysis: Sorting inventory into three groups by value, so the few most valuable A items get the tightest control and the many cheap C items the least.
OPM-04.Cycle counting: Counting a small part of the inventory on a rotating schedule, so everything is checked over time without shutting down for a full count.
OPM-04.Drop shipping: The seller holds no stock. When an order comes in, the supplier ships the product straight to the customer.
OPM-04.Material requirements planning: A computer system that works back from the production schedule to figure out which materials and parts are needed, and when. Known as MRP.
OPM-04.Warehouse management system: Software that directs and records the receiving, storing, picking and shipping of goods inside a warehouse.
OPM-04.Unit control: Tracking inventory by the number of physical units of each item on hand, instead of by its dollar value.
OPM-04.Dollar control: Tracking inventory by its total dollar value instead of by the number of units, used by retailers to plan how much to invest in stock.
OPM-04.Vendor-managed inventory: The supplier watches the buyer's stock levels and decides when and how much to restock.
OPM-04.Consignment: Goods are placed with a seller but still belong to the supplier, who is paid only when they are sold.
OPM-04.Cross-docking: Incoming goods are moved straight from the receiving dock to outgoing trucks, with little or no time in storage.
OPM-04.Open-to-buy: The dollar amount of merchandise a retail buyer can still order for a period without going over the planned inventory budget.
OPM-04.Tickler control: A method in which a small part of the inventory is counted by hand on a regular schedule, prompted by a reminder file.
OPM-04.Weighted average cost: An accounting method that values each unit of inventory at the average cost of all units available for sale.

BCM-01.Email: A message sent electronically over the internet. It is the most common written channel in business, used inside and outside the company.
BCM-01.Business letter: A formal printed message on company letterhead, usually sent to someone outside the organization.
BCM-01.Memo: Short for memorandum. A brief written message for people inside the organization, used for announcements, reminders and requests.
BCM-01.Report: An organized document that presents facts, findings and often recommendations on a topic, such as sales results or project progress.
BCM-01.Text message: A short, informal typed message sent by phone or a chat tool such as Slack, used for quick questions and updates.
BCM-01.Proposal: A document that tries to persuade the reader to approve a project, buy a product or award a contract, explaining the plan and its cost.
BCM-01.Newsletter: A regular publication that shares news and updates with employees or customers.
BCM-01.Business plan: A written document describing a business, its goals, its market and how it will operate and make money. Often written to win funding.
BCM-01.Presentation slides: Pages of brief text and visuals, made in a program such as PowerPoint, that support a talk and can be shared afterward.
BCM-01.Social media post: A short public message on a platform such as LinkedIn or Instagram, used to reach customers and build the brand.
BCM-01.Press release: A written announcement sent to news organizations in the hope that they will report the company's news.
BCM-01.Resume: A one or two page summary of a person's education, work experience and skills, sent to employers when applying for a job.
BCM-01.Meeting agenda: A list of the topics to be covered in a meeting, in order, sent out ahead of time so people can prepare.
BCM-01.Contract: A written agreement that sets out what each party has promised and that a court can enforce.
BCM-01.Invoice: A bill sent by a seller to a buyer listing the goods or services supplied, the amount owed and when payment is due.
BCM-01.Advertisement: A paid written message, such as a print ad, brochure or flyer, that promotes a product or business to the public.
BCM-01.Notice: A short written announcement posted or sent to inform a group of something, such as a policy change or an upcoming event.
BCM-01.Meeting minutes: The official written record of a meeting: who attended, what was discussed and what was decided.
BCM-01.Executive summary: A short overview at the start of a long report or plan that gives busy readers the main points and conclusions.
BCM-01.Employee handbook: A document given to employees that explains the company's policies, rules, benefits and expectations.
BCM-01.Performance review: A written evaluation of how well an employee has done the job over a period, usually prepared by the manager.
BCM-01.Fax: Short for facsimile. A copy of a paper document sent over a telephone line to a machine that prints it at the other end.
BCM-01.Survey: A written set of questions sent to customers or employees to collect their opinions and information.
BCM-01.White paper: An in-depth, authoritative report on a problem or topic, often used by a company to explain an issue and promote its solution.
BCM-01.Letter of intent: A document stating that two parties plan to make a deal and outlining the main terms before a final contract is signed.
BCM-01.Request for quotation: A document asking suppliers to state the price at which they would supply specific goods or services. Known as an RFQ.
BCM-01.Case study: A written account of a real business situation and how it was handled, often used to show how a product solved a customer's problem.
BCM-01.Mission statement: A brief written statement of an organization's purpose: what it does, for whom and why.
BCM-01.Letter to shareholders: A letter from the company's leaders, usually at the front of the annual report, that reviews the year and the outlook for owners.

BCM-02.Language differences: The sender and receiver do not share the same language, or one is far less fluent, so words are missed or misunderstood.
BCM-02.Noise: Sounds and distractions in the surroundings, such as loud machines or interruptions, that make a message hard to hear or follow.
BCM-02.Jargon: Technical terms, acronyms and insider words that people outside a field or company may not understand.
BCM-02.Cultural differences: People from different cultures may read the same words, gestures or level of directness in different ways.
BCM-02.Unclear message: A message that is vague, badly worded or poorly organized, leaving the receiver to guess what the sender meant.
BCM-02.Poor listening: The receiver is not paying full attention, so parts of the message are missed even though they were sent clearly.
BCM-02.Emotions: Strong feelings such as anger, stress or fear can change how a message is worded by the sender and how it is taken by the receiver.
BCM-02.Technology problems: Failures such as a dropped call, a bad internet connection or a broken microphone that stop a message getting through whole.
BCM-02.Wrong channel: Using a method that does not suit the message, such as sending complicated or sensitive news in a short text.
BCM-02.Bias: Fixed opinions or stereotypes about a person or topic that lead a listener to judge the message before really hearing it.
BCM-02.Information overload: Receiving more information than a person can take in, so that important points get lost or ignored.
BCM-02.Physical distance: People who work far apart or in different time zones have fewer chances to talk and cannot easily read each other's reactions.
BCM-02.Lack of trust: A receiver who does not trust or believe the sender is likely to doubt, discount or ignore the message.
BCM-02.Poor timing: A message delivered at a bad moment, such as when the receiver is rushed or upset, is less likely to be taken in.
BCM-02.Conflicting body language: Posture, expression or tone that does not match the spoken words, which leaves the receiver unsure which signal to believe.
BCM-02.Lack of feedback: When the receiver gives no response, the sender cannot tell whether the message was understood and cannot correct mistakes.
BCM-02.Selective perception: People tend to notice what fits their own experience, interests and expectations and to screen out the rest.
BCM-02.Filtering: A sender deliberately holds back or reshapes information, often bad news going up to a boss, so it will look better to the receiver.
BCM-02.Physical disabilities: Conditions such as hearing loss, poor eyesight or a speech impairment that make it harder to send or receive a message without accommodation.
BCM-02.Lack of knowledge: The receiver does not have enough background on the subject to understand the message as the sender intended.
BCM-02.Generational differences: People of different ages may prefer different channels, use different expressions and expect different levels of formality.
BCM-02.Status differences: Gaps in rank can make employees afraid to speak openly to superiors and can make managers slow to listen to those below them.
BCM-02.Semantics: The same word can mean different things to different people, so the receiver may attach a meaning the sender did not intend.
BCM-02.Message length: A message that is too long or rambling buries its main point, and readers or listeners lose interest before reaching it.
BCM-02.Grapevine distortion: Information passed informally from person to person, as rumor or gossip, tends to change and lose accuracy along the way.
BCM-02.Organizational silos: Departments that keep to themselves and do not share information, so news fails to travel across the company.
BCM-02.Ethnocentrism: The belief that one's own culture is the best or the normal one, which leads people to misjudge messages from other cultures.
BCM-02.Internal noise: Distractions inside a person's own mind, such as worries, attitudes or daydreams, that get in the way of taking in a message.

BCM-03.Body language: Messages sent through the way a person moves and holds the body. The study of it is called kinesics.
BCM-03.Facial expressions: Movements of the face, such as a smile, frown or raised eyebrow, that show feelings like happiness, doubt or surprise.
BCM-03.Eye contact: Looking at the person you are communicating with. In U.S. business culture it signals attention, confidence and honesty.
BCM-03.Gestures: Movements of the hands, arms or head that carry meaning, such as pointing, waving, nodding or a thumbs up.
BCM-03.Posture: The way a person sits or stands. Sitting upright and leaning in suggests interest, while slouching suggests boredom.
BCM-03.Tone of voice: How words are said instead of what is said, including pitch, volume, speed and emphasis. Also called paralanguage.
BCM-03.Appearance: Clothing, grooming and overall look, which shape the first impression others form before a word is spoken.
BCM-03.Personal space: The distance people keep between themselves and others. How close someone stands signals the relationship. Its study is called proxemics.
BCM-03.Touch: Physical contact such as a handshake or a pat on the back. Its study is called haptics.
BCM-03.Symbols and signs: Pictures and marks that carry meaning without words, such as logos, icons, emojis and road signs.
BCM-03.Silence: Saying nothing, or pausing, which can signal thought, disagreement, respect or discomfort depending on the situation.
BCM-03.Artifacts: Objects a person wears or displays, such as jewelry, a watch or office decorations, that send messages about status and personality.
BCM-03.Environment: The setting in which communication happens. Room layout, furniture and seating arrangement signal formality and who holds power.
BCM-03.Color: Colors carry meanings and stir feelings, so the colors chosen for clothing, a logo or a room send a message.
BCM-03.Use of time: How a person treats time, such as arriving early or late or replying quickly or slowly, shows respect and priorities. Its study is called chronemics.
BCM-03.Scent: Smells such as perfume, cologne or body odor affect how others see a person. The study of smell in communication is called olfactics.

BCM-04.Salutation: The greeting that opens the letter, such as "Dear Ms. Lopez:". It comes after the inside address and before the body.
BCM-04.Body: The paragraphs that carry the message of the letter, placed between the salutation and the complimentary close.
BCM-04.Signature: The writer's handwritten name, placed above the typed name and job title at the end of the letter.
BCM-04.Complimentary close: The polite phrase that ends the letter, such as "Sincerely," placed after the body and before the signature.
BCM-04.Date: The day the letter was written, with the month spelled out, placed below the heading.
BCM-04.Heading: The sender's name and address at the top of the letter. A printed company letterhead usually serves as the heading.
BCM-04.Inside address: The name, title, company and address of the person receiving the letter, placed above the salutation.
BCM-04.Subject line: An optional line that states in a few words what the letter is about, usually placed near the salutation.
BCM-04.Enclosure notation: A note below the signature, such as "Enclosure" or "Enc.", telling the reader that other documents are included with the letter.
BCM-04.Postscript: A short extra message added after the signature, marked "P.S.". Sales letters often use it to stress a key point.
BCM-04.Attention line: A line that directs the letter to a particular person or department when it is addressed to a whole company.
BCM-04.Copy notation: A note at the end of the letter, marked "cc", listing other people who are being sent a copy.
BCM-04.Reference initials: Initials at the lower left showing who wrote the letter and who typed it, with the typist's in lowercase.
BCM-04.Mailing notation: A note such as "CERTIFIED MAIL" or "CONFIDENTIAL" that tells how the letter was sent or how it should be handled.

BMA-04.Maslow hierarchy of needs: Abraham Maslow's theory that people have five levels of needs, from physical needs and safety up to self-actualization, and are motivated by the lowest level not yet met.
BMA-04.Theory X and Theory Y: Douglas McGregor's two views of workers. Theory X managers assume people dislike work and must be controlled. Theory Y managers assume people like work and seek responsibility.
BMA-04.Herzberg two-factor theory: Frederick Herzberg's finding that hygiene factors such as pay and conditions only prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as achievement and recognition create satisfaction.
BMA-04.Scientific management: Frederick Taylor's approach of studying each job, with time and motion studies, to find the one most efficient way to do it, then training and paying workers accordingly.
BMA-04.Classical management theory: The early school of management thought that focused on efficiency, clear structure and authority. It includes scientific, administrative and bureaucratic management.
BMA-04.Hawthorne effect: The finding from Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies that workers perform better when they receive attention and feel valued, which launched the human relations movement.
BMA-04.Expectancy theory: Victor Vroom's theory that people work hard when they believe effort will lead to good performance, performance will be rewarded and the reward is something they value.
BMA-04.Goal-setting theory: Edwin Locke's theory that specific, challenging goals, combined with feedback, lead to better performance than vague or easy ones.
BMA-04.Management by objectives: Peter Drucker's approach in which managers and employees agree on specific goals together and then review progress against them.
BMA-04.Reinforcement theory: The theory, based on B. F. Skinner's work, that behavior followed by a reward tends to be repeated and behavior followed by a penalty tends to stop.
BMA-04.Equity theory: J. Stacy Adams's theory that employees compare their effort and rewards with those of others and lose motivation when the comparison seems unfair.
BMA-04.Theory Z: William Ouchi's approach, drawing on Japanese practice, that stresses long-term employment, group decision making and concern for the whole employee.
BMA-04.McClelland acquired needs theory: David McClelland's theory that people are driven by three needs learned through experience: achievement, affiliation and power, in different strengths.
BMA-04.Job characteristics model: Hackman and Oldham's model that jobs motivate when they offer skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy and feedback.
BMA-04.Total quality management: A management philosophy, linked to W. Edwards Deming, in which everyone in the organization works on continually improving quality for the customer.
BMA-04.ERG theory: Clayton Alderfer's simplification of Maslow into three groups of needs: existence, relatedness and growth. A person can be motivated by more than one at a time.
BMA-04.Administrative theory: Henri Fayol's theory of how to manage a whole organization, including his 14 principles of management such as unity of command and division of work.
BMA-04.Bureaucratic theory: Max Weber's idea that the most efficient organization has a clear hierarchy, written rules, specialized jobs and promotion based on merit.
BMA-04.Contingency theory: The view that there is no single best way to manage or lead. The right approach depends on the situation.
BMA-04.Systems theory: The view of an organization as a set of connected parts that takes in inputs, transforms them and sends out outputs, so a change in one part affects the others.
BMA-04.Self-determination theory: Deci and Ryan's theory that people are most motivated from within when their needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness are met.
BMA-04.Path-goal theory: Robert House's theory that a leader's job is to clear the path for followers to reach their goals, by giving the direction and support the situation calls for.

BMA-05.Schedule: A list of the project's tasks with their start dates, end dates and deadlines, showing when each piece of work must be done.
BMA-05.Budget: An estimate of what the project will cost, broken down by item, used to approve spending and to track it as work goes on.
BMA-05.Gantt chart: A bar chart that shows each task as a horizontal bar along a calendar, so the timing and overlap of tasks can be seen at a glance.
BMA-05.To-do list: A simple list of the tasks that need doing, ticked off as each one is completed.
BMA-05.Spreadsheet: A table in a program such as Excel, used to list tasks, dates, costs and who is responsible, and to do the calculations.
BMA-05.Project management software: A program such as Trello, Asana or Microsoft Project that lets a team assign tasks, set deadlines and track progress in one place.
BMA-05.Milestones: Key checkpoints in a project, such as finishing a design or passing a test, used to measure whether the work is on track.
BMA-05.Project plan: The master document that describes how the project will be carried out, including its tasks, timing, resources and responsibilities.
BMA-05.Flowchart: A diagram of boxes and arrows that shows the order of steps or tasks and how each one leads to the next.
BMA-05.Meeting agenda: A list of the topics a project meeting will cover, shared in advance to keep the discussion focused and on time.
BMA-05.Status report: A regular update that tells managers and stakeholders what has been finished, what is behind and what problems have come up.
BMA-05.Work breakdown structure: A chart that splits the whole project into smaller and smaller pieces of work until each piece is easy to assign, schedule and cost.
BMA-05.Kanban board: A board with columns such as To Do, Doing and Done, on which a card for each task is moved along as the work progresses.
BMA-05.Project proposal: A document written before the project starts that explains what it would do, why it is worth doing and what it would cost, to win approval.
BMA-05.Goals and objectives: Clear statements of what the project is meant to achieve, ideally specific and measurable, against which success is judged.
BMA-05.Communication plan: A document setting out who needs what information about the project, how often, in what form and from whom.
BMA-05.PERT chart: Program Evaluation and Review Technique: a network diagram of tasks and the order they depend on, with time estimates used to predict how long the project will take.
BMA-05.Critical path method: A technique that finds the longest chain of dependent tasks in a project. Any delay on that chain delays the finish date.
BMA-05.Project charter: A short document that formally authorizes the project, naming its purpose, main goals, sponsor and project manager.
BMA-05.Scope statement: A written description of exactly what the project will and will not deliver, used to stop extra work creeping in.
BMA-05.Resource plan: A plan listing the people, equipment and materials the project needs and when each will be needed.
BMA-05.Contingency plan: A backup plan prepared in advance, saying what the team will do if a particular problem or risk actually happens.
BMA-05.Timesheets: Records of the hours each person spends on each task, used to track labor costs and compare actual effort with the plan.
BMA-05.Risk register: A list of the things that could go wrong in a project, with how likely and how serious each is and what will be done about it.
BMA-05.RACI chart: A table showing, for each task, who is Responsible for doing it, who is Accountable, who must be Consulted and who must be Informed.
