ECO-07.UNCTAD: The United Nations Conference on Trade and Development: a United Nations body that helps developing countries benefit from trade and investment.

BA-07.Lay off employees: Ending the jobs of some workers so the payroll is smaller. Labor is often the largest cost a business has.
BA-07.Save energy: Using less electricity, heating and fuel, for example with efficient lighting and equipment, so utility bills fall.
BA-07.Negotiate with suppliers: Asking suppliers for lower prices or better terms, or switching to a cheaper supplier, so materials and goods cost less.
BA-07.Outsourcing: Paying an outside company to do a task, such as payroll or cleaning, when it can do the work for less than in-house staff.
BA-07.Automation: Using machines or software to do work that people did by hand, which lowers the labor cost of each task.
BA-07.Reduce waste: Using fewer materials and throwing less away, so the business pays for less that never reaches a customer.
BA-07.Buy in bulk: Ordering larger quantities at one time to earn a lower price per unit from the supplier.
BA-07.Cut employee hours: Scheduling fewer hours or limiting overtime so the business pays less in wages without ending jobs.
BA-07.Remote work: Letting employees work from home, which can reduce the office space, utilities and supplies the business pays for.
BA-07.Cheaper or smaller premises: Moving to a lower-rent location, giving up unused space or closing a site, so the business pays less for rent and upkeep.
BA-07.Reduce inventory: Keeping less stock on hand, which lowers the cost of storing, insuring and financing goods that are waiting to be sold.
BA-07.Cut travel: Replacing business trips with video meetings or setting tighter travel rules, which saves on airfare, hotels and meals.
BA-07.Hiring freeze: A decision to stop filling open jobs for a time, so payroll shrinks as people leave without anyone being laid off.
BA-07.Cut advertising spending: Spending less on promotion or moving to cheaper media. It saves money now but can reduce sales later.
BA-07.Cut pay or benefits: Lowering or freezing wages, bonuses or benefits. It saves money quickly but can hurt morale and push good workers to leave.
BA-07.Go paperless: Keeping and sending documents electronically, which saves on paper, printing, postage and storage space.
BA-07.Streamline processes: Removing steps that add no value so the same work takes less time and fewer resources.
BA-07.Buy used or lease equipment: Getting equipment secondhand or renting it instead of buying it new, which lowers what the business pays for it.
BA-07.Budgeting and expense tracking: Setting spending limits and comparing actual spending against them, so overspending is noticed and corrected early.
BA-07.Preventive maintenance: Servicing equipment on a regular schedule so it lasts longer and expensive breakdowns are avoided.
BA-07.Cross-train employees: Teaching workers to do more than one job, so the business can cover absences and busy periods with fewer people.
BA-07.Offshoring: Moving work to a country where wages and other costs are lower. It differs from outsourcing, which means paying another company to do the work.
BA-07.Reduce employee turnover: Keeping workers longer, because recruiting, hiring and training a replacement each time someone leaves is expensive.
BA-07.Reduce shrinkage: Cutting the loss of inventory to theft, damage and errors, so the business does not pay for goods it never sells.
BA-07.Drop unprofitable products: Ending products or services that cost more to make and sell than they bring in.
BA-07.Reduce defects and rework: Getting work right the first time, which saves the materials and labor spent on fixing or replacing faulty products.

BA-08.Employee records: Files on each worker, such as the job application, pay history, performance reviews and emergency contacts. Also called personnel records.
BA-08.Tax records: Copies of the tax returns a business has filed and the documents that support the numbers on them.
BA-08.Sales records: Details of what was sold, when, to whom and for how much. They show which products and time periods bring in the most money.
BA-08.Invoices and receipts: Bills the business has sent or received and proof of what has been paid. They back up the entries in the accounting records.
BA-08.Accounting records: The books of the business, such as its journals and ledgers and the financial statements built from them, which show what it earned, spent, owns and owes.
BA-08.Payroll records: Records of the hours each employee worked, the wages paid and the taxes and other amounts withheld from each paycheck.
BA-08.Customer records: Information about customers, such as contact details and purchase history, often kept in a customer database.
BA-08.Inventory records: Records of which goods the business has in stock, how many, and what they cost.
BA-08.Contracts: Signed agreements with customers, suppliers, landlords and others. Keeping them lets the business prove what each side promised.
BA-08.Bank statements: Reports from the bank listing every deposit, withdrawal and fee on an account. The business checks them against its own books.
BA-08.Licenses and permits: Official documents that show the business is allowed to operate or to carry out a certain activity.
BA-08.Insurance policies: The contracts with insurance companies that state what losses are covered, for how much and at what price.
BA-08.Meeting minutes: The official written record of what was discussed and decided at a meeting, such as a meeting of the board of directors.
BA-08.Budgets: Written plans of expected income and spending for a period, kept so actual results can be compared against them.
BA-08.Safety records: Logs of workplace accidents, injuries and safety inspections. Many employers are required by law to keep them.
BA-08.Formation documents: The papers that created the business and set its rules, such as articles of incorporation, bylaws or a partnership agreement.
BA-08.Correspondence: Letters, emails and memos the business has sent and received, kept as a record of what was communicated.
BA-08.Training records: Records of which employees completed which training and when, including any certifications they hold.
BA-08.Supplier records: Information about the companies the business buys from, such as contact details, prices, terms and past orders.
BA-08.Job applications and resumes: The documents submitted by people who applied for jobs, kept as a record of how hiring decisions were made.
BA-08.Policies and procedures: The written rules of the business and step-by-step instructions for doing its work, often collected in a manual or handbook.
BA-08.Shipping records: Documents showing what was shipped or received, when and by which carrier, such as bills of lading and packing slips.
BA-08.Property and equipment records: Records of the buildings, land, vehicles and equipment the business owns, including what each cost and proof of ownership.
BA-08.Maintenance records: Logs of the service and repairs carried out on equipment, vehicles and buildings.
BA-08.New-hire forms: Government forms completed when a worker is hired, such as the form that verifies the right to work in the country and the tax withholding form.
BA-08.Intellectual property records: Proof that the business owns its creations, such as patent, trademark and copyright registrations.
BA-08.Customer complaint records: A log of the problems customers have reported and how each was resolved, used to spot repeat issues.
BA-08.Shareholder records: A corporation's list of who owns its shares and how many each person holds.

BA-09.Receptionist: The person at the front desk who greets visitors, answers the main phone line and directs people to the right place.
BA-09.Administrative assistant: A worker who supports a team or office by handling schedules, documents, calls and other routine tasks. Formerly called a secretary.
BA-09.Office manager: The person responsible for keeping an office running smoothly, including supplies, equipment and the support staff.
BA-09.Executive assistant: A high-level assistant who supports one senior leader by managing the calendar, travel, messages and confidential documents.
BA-09.Data entry clerk: A worker who types information from forms and other documents into a computer system quickly and accurately.
BA-09.Bookkeeper: A worker who records the daily money transactions of a business, such as sales, bills and payments.
BA-09.Customer service representative: A worker who answers customer questions and solves problems with orders or accounts by phone, email or chat.
BA-09.Office clerk: A worker who does a mix of general office tasks, such as filing, copying, answering phones and sorting mail.
BA-09.Payroll clerk: A worker who collects the hours employees worked and prepares their pay so that everyone is paid correctly and on time.
BA-09.File clerk: A worker who organizes, stores and retrieves the paper and electronic records of a business.
BA-09.Human resources assistant: A worker who supports the human resources department by keeping employee records and helping with hiring paperwork.
BA-09.Mail clerk: A worker who sorts and delivers incoming mail and packages and prepares outgoing mail for a business.
BA-09.Switchboard operator: A worker who answers incoming calls for an organization and transfers each one to the right person or department.
BA-09.Scheduler: A worker who sets up appointments, meetings or work shifts and keeps the calendars up to date.
BA-09.Administrative services manager: A manager who plans and directs the support services of an organization, such as record keeping, mail and office supplies.
BA-09.Virtual assistant: An administrative assistant who works remotely, often as an independent contractor serving several clients online.
BA-09.Medical secretary: An administrative assistant in a doctor's office or hospital who schedules patients and handles medical records and billing forms.
BA-09.Legal secretary: An administrative assistant in a law office who prepares legal documents, files papers with courts and keeps the lawyers' calendars.
BA-09.Project coordinator: A worker who supports a project manager by tracking tasks and deadlines, arranging meetings and keeping project documents in order.
BA-09.Shipping and receiving clerk: A worker who keeps records of the goods a business sends out and takes in and checks them against the orders.
BA-09.Records manager: The person in charge of how an organization stores, protects, finds and finally disposes of its records.
BA-09.Transcriptionist: A worker who listens to recorded speech, such as dictation or meetings, and types it into a written document.
BA-09.Word processor: As a job title, a worker who types, formats and edits documents such as letters and reports. Also called a typist.
BA-09.Procurement clerk: A worker who prepares purchase orders, keeps track of what has been ordered and checks that the goods arrive.
BA-09.Dispatcher: A worker who schedules and sends out drivers, service technicians or emergency crews and keeps a record of each call.
BA-09.Office courier: A worker who carries documents and packages between offices or to other businesses. Also called a messenger.

BCM-07.Staff meeting: A regular meeting of a manager and the people on the team to share news, review work and raise problems.
BCM-07.Board meeting: A formal meeting of the board of directors of a company, where major decisions are voted on and recorded in minutes.
BCM-07.Brainstorming session: A meeting held to come up with as many ideas as possible, with judgment of the ideas saved for later.
BCM-07.Training session: A meeting in which employees are taught new knowledge or skills, such as how to use a new system.
BCM-07.One-on-one meeting: A private meeting between two people, usually a manager and one employee, to talk about progress, problems and goals.
BCM-07.Video conference: A meeting held over video or phone so that people in different places can take part without traveling.
BCM-07.Client meeting: A meeting with a customer or possible customer to learn what they need, present a proposal or review the work being done for them.
BCM-07.Annual shareholders meeting: A yearly meeting at which the owners of a corporation hear reports from its leaders and vote on matters such as who sits on the board.
BCM-07.Project kickoff meeting: The first meeting of a project team, held to agree on the goals, roles, schedule and next steps.
BCM-07.Status update meeting: A meeting in which team members report what is done, what is next and what is in the way, so a project stays on track.
BCM-07.Committee meeting: A meeting of a small group that has been given one particular job, such as planning an event or reviewing safety.
BCM-07.All-hands meeting: A meeting of everyone in the company, used by leaders to share results and plans and to take questions. Also called a town hall.
BCM-07.Performance review meeting: A meeting in which a manager and an employee discuss how well the employee has done the job and set goals for the next period.
BCM-07.Planning meeting: A meeting held to set goals and decide how to reach them, such as a session on the strategy for the coming year.
BCM-07.Sales meeting: A meeting of the sales team to review results against targets, share leads and learn about new products or promotions.
BCM-07.Conference: A large gathering, often lasting several days, where people from one industry or company meet to hear speakers and exchange ideas.
BCM-07.Stand-up meeting: A very short daily meeting, often held standing, in which each person says what they are working on and what is blocking them.
BCM-07.Problem-solving meeting: A meeting called to find the cause of one particular problem and agree on how to fix it.
BCM-07.Decision-making meeting: A meeting held so that a group can weigh the options on a question and reach a final choice.
BCM-07.Retreat: A meeting held away from the workplace, often for a full day or more, so a team can focus on planning or working together.
BCM-07.Negotiation meeting: A meeting in which two sides with different interests discuss terms and try to reach an agreement both can accept.
BCM-07.Webinar: A seminar presented over the internet. A speaker presents to an online audience that can usually send in questions.
BCM-07.Team-building meeting: A meeting built around activities that help coworkers get to know and trust one another so they work together better.
BCM-07.Informational meeting: A meeting held mainly to pass information to a group, such as an announcement of a new policy.
BCM-07.Management meeting: A meeting of the managers or top executives of a business to review performance and coordinate their departments.
BCM-07.Emergency meeting: An unplanned meeting called at short notice to deal with an urgent problem or crisis.
BCM-07.Retrospective: A meeting held after a project or event to discuss what went well, what did not and what to do differently next time.
BCM-07.Press conference: A meeting to which reporters are invited so that a company can make an announcement and answer their questions.
BCM-07.Working lunch: A meeting held over a meal so that people can discuss business without taking extra time out of the workday.

BCM-08.Maintain eye contact: Looking at the speaker while they talk, which shows you are paying attention and helps you stay focused on the message.
BCM-08.Do not interrupt: Letting the speaker finish the thought before you respond, so you hear the whole message and the speaker feels respected.
BCM-08.Ask questions: Asking the speaker to explain or expand on a point, which clears up anything you did not understand and shows interest.
BCM-08.Nod: Moving your head up and down now and then to signal, without words, that you are following what is being said.
BCM-08.Paraphrase: Saying the speaker's message back in your own words so that the speaker can confirm or correct what you understood.
BCM-08.Avoid distractions: Putting away your phone, closing other work and tuning out noise so your attention stays on the speaker.
BCM-08.Take notes: Writing down the key points as you listen, which keeps you focused and gives you a record to check later.
BCM-08.Summarize: Briefly restating the main points at the end of a conversation to make sure both sides agree on what was said.
BCM-08.Pay attention: Giving the speaker your full focus instead of letting your mind wander. It is the starting point for all active listening.
BCM-08.Use open body language: Facing the speaker, leaning in slightly and keeping your arms uncrossed, which signals that you are open to the message.
BCM-08.Give verbal affirmations: Using short responses such as "I see" or "go on" that encourage the speaker to continue without taking over the conversation.
BCM-08.Give feedback: Responding to the speaker in a way that shows you understood, for example with a thoughtful comment or answer.
BCM-08.Show empathy: Trying to understand the speaker's feelings and point of view, and letting the speaker know that you do.
BCM-08.Withhold judgment: Keeping an open mind and hearing the whole message before deciding whether you agree with it.
BCM-08.Watch nonverbal cues: Noticing the speaker's tone of voice, facial expressions and body language, which often show feelings the words leave out.
BCM-08.Allow silence: Staying quiet through pauses so the speaker has time to think and finish, instead of rushing to fill the gap.
BCM-08.Reflect feelings: Putting into words the emotion you hear, for example "that sounds frustrating", so the speaker knows the feeling was understood.
BCM-08.Show interest with facial expressions: Letting your face respond to what is said, for example with a smile or a look of concern, so the speaker can see you are engaged.
BCM-08.Listen for main ideas: Focusing on the central points the speaker is making instead of getting lost in every small detail.
BCM-08.Do not plan your reply while listening: Waiting until the speaker has finished before working out your answer, because rehearsing a reply makes you miss part of the message.
BCM-08.Prepare to listen: Getting ready before a conversation or meeting by clearing your mind and deciding what you need to learn from it.
BCM-08.Remember what was said: Holding on to the key points after the conversation so you can act on them. Many models count it as a stage of listening.

BCM-09.Introduction: The opening section, which tells the reader what the report is about, why it was written and how it is organized.
BCM-09.Conclusion: The section that states what the findings mean. It draws the evidence together but adds no new information.
BCM-09.Title page: The first page, showing the title of the report, who wrote it, who it was written for and the date.
BCM-09.Table of contents: A list of the sections of the report with their page numbers, so a reader can find any part quickly.
BCM-09.Body: The main part of the report, where the facts, findings and analysis are presented under headings.
BCM-09.Executive summary: A short overview at the front of the report that gives the main findings, conclusions and recommendations for a busy reader.
BCM-09.Recommendations: The section that says what actions the writer thinks the reader should take, based on the conclusions.
BCM-09.References: A list of the sources the writer used, so readers can check the facts and the original authors get credit.
BCM-09.Appendix: A section at the back holding supporting material, such as raw data or survey forms, that is too detailed for the body.
BCM-09.Methodology: The section that explains how the information was gathered, for example through surveys, interviews or company records.
BCM-09.List of illustrations: A page near the front that lists the tables, charts and other figures in the report with their page numbers.
BCM-09.Letter of transmittal: A short letter or memo that hands the finished report to the person who asked for it and points out its key results.
BCM-09.Glossary: An alphabetical list of the technical terms used in the report, each with its meaning.
BCM-09.Scope and limitations: A statement of what the report covers and does not cover, and of anything that limited the research, such as time or data.
BCM-09.Statement of purpose: A sentence or short section that states the problem the report addresses or the question it sets out to answer.
BCM-09.Index: An alphabetical list of topics at the very end of a long report, with the pages where each is mentioned.
BCM-09.Letter of authorization: The letter or memo in which someone with authority asked for the report to be written. A copy may be placed at the front.
BCM-09.Title fly: A plain sheet carrying only the title of the report, placed before the title page in the most formal reports.
BCM-09.Acknowledgments: A short section thanking the people and organizations that helped the writer with the report.
BCM-09.Letter of acceptance: The writer's reply agreeing to prepare the report that was requested. Some very formal reports include a copy at the front.
BCM-09.Preface: A short opening note, in some long reports, that explains how the report came to be written. A foreword does a similar job.

BCM-10.Work experience: A list of the jobs you have held, usually starting with the most recent, showing where you worked and what you did there.
BCM-10.Education: The schools you attended and the diplomas or degrees you earned or are working toward.
BCM-10.Contact information: Your phone number, email address and location, placed at the top so an employer can reach you easily.
BCM-10.Name: Your full name, shown in the largest type at the very top of the resume so the reader knows at once whose it is.
BCM-10.Skills: A list of the abilities you bring to the job, such as software you can use, equipment you can run or strengths in working with people.
BCM-10.References: People who can speak for your work and character. Most applicants now give them on a separate sheet when the employer asks.
BCM-10.Objective: One or two sentences near the top that say what kind of job you are looking for.
BCM-10.Awards and honors: Recognition you have earned, such as honor roll, scholarships or competition wins, which shows that others have noticed your work.
BCM-10.Volunteer experience: Unpaid work you have done for a community group, charity or school, which shows skills and character even without paid jobs.
BCM-10.Activities: Clubs, sports and other organizations you take part in outside class, which show teamwork and commitment.
BCM-10.Certifications: Official proof that you passed a test or course in a skill, such as first aid or a software program, or hold a license for a job.
BCM-10.Summary: A short paragraph near the top that highlights your strongest skills and experience for the job you want.
BCM-10.Grade point average: The average of your school grades. Students often include it when it is strong and they have little work experience.
BCM-10.Leadership positions: Roles in which you led others, such as club president or team captain, listed to show responsibility.
BCM-10.Languages: The languages you can speak or write besides English and how well you know each one.
BCM-10.Job titles: The name of the position you held at each employer, such as cashier or shift leader.
BCM-10.Dates of employment: The month and year you started and left each job, which show how long you stayed and whether there are gaps.
BCM-10.Relevant coursework: School classes that relate to the job you want, listed by students who have little work experience.
BCM-10.Internships: Short-term work placements, paid or unpaid, completed to gain experience in a career field.
BCM-10.Employer names: The name and location of each business you worked for, listed with each job in the work experience section.
BCM-10.Job duties: Short bullet points under each job that describe what you were responsible for and what you achieved.
BCM-10.Hobbies and interests: Things you enjoy outside work or school. They are optional and are most useful when they relate to the job.
BCM-10.Professional memberships: The career-related organizations you belong to, such as a trade association or a student organization.
BCM-10.Projects: Major pieces of work you completed in school or on your own that show skills the job requires.
BCM-10.Portfolio link: A web address for samples of your work or for your professional profile, so an employer can see more than the page holds.
BCM-10.Publications: Articles or other work you have written that have been published, listed mainly on academic and professional resumes.
BCM-10.Military service: Time served in the armed forces, including the branch, rank and duties, which employers count as work experience.
BCM-10.Expected graduation date: The month and year you plan to finish school, which tells an employer when you will be available for full-time work.

LAW-07.Contract law: The rules on how legally binding agreements are made and enforced. A business relies on it in every deal with customers, suppliers and workers.
LAW-07.Tax law: The rules on what taxes a business owes, such as income, payroll and sales taxes, and how and when it must report and pay them.
LAW-07.Employment law: The rules on how employers must treat workers, covering matters such as wages, hours, discrimination and the right to form a union.
LAW-07.Intellectual property law: The rules that protect creations of the mind, such as inventions, brand names and written works, through patents, trademarks and copyrights.
LAW-07.Environmental law: The rules that limit pollution and control how a business uses natural resources and disposes of waste.
LAW-07.Consumer protection law: The rules that guard buyers against unsafe products and unfair or deceptive selling practices.
LAW-07.Antitrust law: The rules that keep markets competitive by banning practices such as price fixing between rivals and mergers that would wipe out competition.
LAW-07.Tort law: The rules on civil wrongs that harm another person, such as negligence. It lets an injured customer sue a business for damages.
LAW-07.Criminal law: The rules that define offenses against society, such as fraud and embezzlement, and their punishments. A business can be a victim or a defendant.
LAW-07.Property law: The rules on owning, leasing and using land, buildings and other property, including zoning rules on where a business may locate.
LAW-07.Corporate law: The rules on how corporations and other business entities are formed, run and dissolved, and on the duties of their directors and officers.
LAW-07.Workplace safety law: The rules that require employers to keep the workplace free of serious hazards and to record injuries.
LAW-07.Bankruptcy law: The federal rules for a business or person that cannot pay its debts, allowing it to reorganize or to sell assets and pay creditors.
LAW-07.Securities law: The rules on selling stocks and bonds to investors, which require companies to disclose honest information and ban insider trading.
LAW-07.Advertising law: The rules that require advertising claims to be truthful and supported by evidence and that ban deceptive promotions.
LAW-07.Civil law: The broad branch of law that settles disputes between private parties, such as a lawsuit over a broken contract, as opposed to criminal cases.
LAW-07.Product liability law: The rules that hold makers and sellers responsible when a defective product injures someone.
LAW-07.International trade law: The rules on importing and exporting, including customs duties, trade agreements and limits on what may cross a border.
LAW-07.Privacy law: The rules on how a business may collect, store, use and share personal information about customers and employees.
LAW-07.Agency law: The rules on when one person, the agent, can act for another, the principal. It makes a business responsible for what its employees do on the job.
LAW-07.Sales law: The rules on contracts for selling goods. In the United States they are set out mainly in the Uniform Commercial Code.
LAW-07.Licensing law: The state and local rules that require a business or a profession to hold a license or permit before it may operate.
LAW-07.Administrative law: The rules made and enforced by government agencies, and the rules those agencies themselves must follow.
LAW-07.Constitutional law: The law that comes from the Constitution. It gives Congress the power to regulate trade between states and limits what government may do to a business.
LAW-07.Immigration law: The rules on who may enter and work in the country. Employers must confirm that each person they hire is allowed to work.
LAW-07.Insurance law: The rules on insurance policies and insurance companies, including what coverage some businesses are required to carry.
LAW-07.Banking law: The rules on how banks and other lenders operate, which affect how a business borrows money and handles payments.
LAW-07.Franchise law: The rules on selling franchises, including the information a franchisor must give a buyer before the deal is signed.
LAW-07.Cyber law: The rules that apply to computers and the internet, covering matters such as online contracts, hacking and digital signatures.

LAW-08.Trial: The court hearing at which both sides present evidence and arguments to a judge or jury, who then decide the case.
LAW-08.Verdict: The decision the jury reaches at the end of the trial on whether the defendant is liable and, if so, for how much.
LAW-08.Complaint: The document that starts a lawsuit. In it the plaintiff states what the defendant did wrong and what remedy the plaintiff wants.
LAW-08.Appeal: A request by the losing side for a higher court to review the case for legal errors made in the trial court.
LAW-08.Settlement: An agreement between the two sides that ends the dispute without a court decision, usually with one side paying the other.
LAW-08.Discovery: The stage before trial in which each side must share its evidence with the other through written questions, documents and depositions, which are sworn out-of-court interviews of witnesses.
LAW-08.Jury selection: The process of questioning possible jurors and choosing the ones who will hear the case. Its legal name is voir dire.
LAW-08.Opening statements: The speeches at the start of a trial in which each lawyer tells the judge or jury what the evidence is expected to show.
LAW-08.Closing arguments: The final speeches of a trial, in which each lawyer sums up the evidence and argues for a decision in the client's favor.
LAW-08.Judgment: The court's official final decision in the case, which states who won and what the loser must pay or do.
LAW-08.Summons: The official notice delivered to the defendant saying that a lawsuit has been filed and that a response is due by a deadline.
LAW-08.Answer: The defendant's written reply to the complaint, admitting or denying each claim and raising any defenses.
LAW-08.Presentation of evidence: The main part of the trial, in which each side calls witnesses and shows documents, and the other side may cross-examine.
LAW-08.Mediation or arbitration: An attempt to end the dispute without a trial. A mediator helps the two sides reach their own agreement, while an arbitrator hears both sides and decides. Courts often require one first.
LAW-08.Pretrial conference: A meeting of the judge and the lawyers before trial to narrow the issues, set the schedule and explore a settlement.
LAW-08.Pretrial motions: Formal requests to the judge before trial, such as a request to dismiss the case or to decide it without a trial.
LAW-08.Jury deliberation: The private discussion in which the jurors weigh the evidence after the trial and work toward a verdict.
LAW-08.Jury instructions: The judge's explanation to the jurors of the law they must apply to the facts when they decide the case.
LAW-08.Enforcement of judgment: The steps the winner takes to collect if the loser does not pay, such as having money taken from the loser's wages or bank account.
LAW-08.Pleadings: The first stage of a lawsuit, made up of the written statements each side files with the court: the complaint and the answer.
LAW-08.Counterclaim: A claim the defendant files against the plaintiff in the same lawsuit, saying that the plaintiff also did something wrong.
LAW-08.Post-trial motions: Requests made to the trial judge after the verdict, such as a request for a new trial.
LAW-08.Default judgment: A judgment for the plaintiff that the court enters when the defendant fails to respond to the lawsuit in time.
LAW-08.Subpoena: A court order that requires a person to appear and testify or to hand over documents for the case.

LAW-09.Compensatory damages: Money awarded to make up for the loss the injured side actually suffered, such as repair bills, medical costs or lost income. It is the most common remedy.
LAW-09.Punitive damages: Extra money awarded to punish a defendant whose conduct was especially bad and to warn others. They are given in some tort cases and almost never for a simple breach of contract.
LAW-09.Injunction: A court order telling a party to stop doing something, or sometimes to do something, such as an order to stop using a rival's trademark.
LAW-09.Specific performance: A court order requiring a party to do exactly what the contract promised. It is used when the subject is unique, such as land or a rare item, so money would not be enough.
LAW-09.Nominal damages: A very small sum, such as one dollar, awarded when a legal right was violated but no real financial loss was shown.
LAW-09.Restitution: An order to give back money or property that one side received unfairly, so that each side is returned to where it stood before.
LAW-09.Attorney fees and court costs: Payment of the winning side's lawyer bills and filing costs by the loser. In the United States each side usually pays its own lawyer unless a law or the contract says otherwise.
LAW-09.Rescission: Cancellation of a contract so that both sides are released from it, used for example when one side was tricked into signing.
LAW-09.Liquidated damages: An amount the two sides agreed in the contract itself would be paid if one of them broke it. A court enforces it if the amount is a reasonable estimate and not a penalty.
LAW-09.Consequential damages: Money for losses that follow indirectly from the wrong, such as sales lost because a late delivery shut a factory, if the loss could have been foreseen.
LAW-09.Incidental damages: Money for the extra costs the injured side ran up in dealing with a breach, such as storing or shipping rejected goods or arranging a replacement.
LAW-09.Reformation: A court order rewriting a written contract so that it states what the two sides actually agreed, used to fix a mistake in the document.
LAW-09.Declaratory judgment: A court ruling that states the legal rights and duties of each side without ordering anyone to pay or act, which can settle a dispute early.
LAW-09.Treble damages: Damages multiplied by three, which certain laws allow as a penalty. Federal antitrust law lets a business harmed by illegal price fixing collect them.
LAW-09.Interest: Money added to an award to make up for the time the winner had to wait to be paid, both before and after the judgment.
LAW-09.Statutory damages: An amount fixed by a law instead of by proof of the actual loss. Copyright law, for example, lets an owner choose a set sum for each work that was copied.
LAW-09.Replevin: A court order that returns particular goods to their rightful owner, used when the owner wants the property itself back and not its value in money.
LAW-09.Constructive trust: A remedy in which a court treats a person who wrongly obtained property as holding it for the rightful owner, and orders it handed over.
LAW-09.Quantum meruit: Payment of the reasonable value of work or goods that one side provided when there was no enforceable contract, so the other side is not enriched for free.

BMA-08.Pay raises: A permanent increase in an employee's wage or salary, often given for good performance or long service.
BMA-08.Recognition: Noticing and praising good work, in private or in public, for example with a thank-you or an employee of the month award.
BMA-08.Bonuses: Extra pay on top of regular wages, given for reaching a target or for a strong result by the worker, the team or the company.
BMA-08.Promotions: Moving an employee up to a job with more responsibility, status and usually pay. The chance to advance gives people a reason to work hard.
BMA-08.Benefits: Rewards other than pay, such as health insurance, retirement plans and perks, that make employees want to stay and do well.
BMA-08.Flexible schedules: Letting employees have a say in when or where they work, which helps them balance the job with the rest of their lives.
BMA-08.Training and development: Giving employees the chance to learn new skills and grow in their careers, which shows the company is investing in them.
BMA-08.Positive work environment: A workplace that is safe, pleasant and supportive, where people get along and want to come to work.
BMA-08.Clear goals: Targets that are specific and challenging but reachable. People work harder when they know exactly what they are aiming for.
BMA-08.Paid time off: Extra vacation days or other paid leave, offered as a reward or to help employees rest and return with more energy.
BMA-08.Feedback: Regular information from a manager about how well an employee is doing and how to improve, so effort is pointed in the right direction.
BMA-08.Empowerment: Giving employees the authority to make decisions about their own work, which builds a sense of ownership and trust.
BMA-08.Team building: Activities and events that help coworkers bond, which makes people feel they belong and want to pull their weight for the group.
BMA-08.Open communication: Keeping employees informed and listening to their ideas and concerns, so they feel respected and part of the company.
BMA-08.Employee involvement: Asking employees for their input on decisions that affect their work, which increases their commitment to making those decisions succeed.
BMA-08.Job enrichment: Redesigning a job to add responsibility, challenge and control over how the work is done, so the work itself is more rewarding.
BMA-08.Job rotation: Moving employees between different jobs from time to time, which reduces boredom and teaches them new skills.
BMA-08.Job enlargement: Adding more tasks at the same level to a job so the work is more varied and less repetitive.
BMA-08.Fair treatment: Applying rules, pay and rewards evenly and treating everyone with respect. People lose motivation when they feel they are treated unfairly.
BMA-08.Lead by example: A manager showing the effort, attitude and behavior expected of the team, which earns respect and sets the standard.
BMA-08.Job security: Confidence that the job will last. Workers who are not afraid of losing their jobs can focus on doing them well.
BMA-08.Stock ownership: Giving employees shares in the company or the right to buy them, so that they gain when the company does well.
BMA-08.Contests: Friendly competitions, such as a prize for the most sales in a month, that make reaching a target more exciting.
BMA-08.Shared vision: Explaining where the company is going and why the work matters, so employees feel they are part of something worth the effort.
BMA-08.Gainsharing: A plan that pays a group of employees a share of the money saved when they raise productivity or cut costs.
BMA-08.Status rewards: Signs of rank, such as a better job title or a larger office, that reward an employee with respect instead of money.

BMA-09.Business plan: A written document that describes a business, its market, how it will operate and its expected finances. It guides the owners and is shown to lenders and investors.
BMA-09.Strategic plan: A long-term plan made by top management that sets the overall direction and major goals of the whole company.
BMA-09.Marketing plan: A plan that sets out who the target customers are and how the business will reach them through its product, price, place and promotion choices.
BMA-09.Budget: A financial plan that estimates the money coming in and going out over a period and sets limits on spending.
BMA-09.Operational plan: A short-term plan that spells out the day-to-day activities needed to carry out the larger plans of the company.
BMA-09.Tactical plan: A medium-term plan, usually made by middle managers, that turns the company strategy into specific goals for a department.
BMA-09.Contingency plan: A backup plan that says what the business will do if things do not go as expected, such as a supplier failing to deliver.
BMA-09.Project plan: A plan for one piece of work with a clear start and end, listing its tasks, schedule, budget and who is responsible.
BMA-09.Emergency plan: A plan that tells employees what to do in a fire, severe weather or other danger, including how to leave the building.
BMA-09.Crisis management plan: A plan for how leaders will respond and communicate if an event such as a scandal or product recall threatens the company.
BMA-09.Succession plan: A plan that identifies and prepares the people who will take over key positions when the current leaders leave.
BMA-09.Staffing plan: A plan that forecasts how many workers with which skills the business will need and how it will hire or train them.
BMA-09.Action plan: A list of the specific steps needed to reach a goal, with who will do each one and by when.
BMA-09.Sales plan: A plan that sets sales targets for a period and describes how the sales team will reach them.
BMA-09.Production plan: A plan for what goods will be made, in what quantity and when, so that materials, machines and workers are ready.
BMA-09.Business continuity plan: A plan for keeping the most important parts of the business running during and after a major disruption.
BMA-09.Disaster recovery plan: A plan for restoring computer systems, data and operations after an event such as a flood, fire or cyberattack.
BMA-09.Single-use plan: A plan made for a one-time situation, such as a project or a store opening, that is not used again once the work is done.
BMA-09.Standing plan: A plan used again and again for situations that keep coming up. Policies, procedures and rules are the main kinds.
BMA-09.Exit plan: A plan for how the owner will eventually leave the business, for example by selling it or passing it to a family member.
BMA-09.Training plan: A plan that sets out what employees need to learn, how they will be taught and when the training will take place.
BMA-09.Communication plan: A plan that sets out who needs what information, when they will receive it and through which channel.
BMA-09.Capital expenditure plan: A plan for large, long-term purchases such as buildings, machinery and vehicles, and for how they will be paid for.
BMA-09.Risk management plan: A plan that lists the risks a business or project faces and how each will be avoided, reduced, transferred or accepted.
BMA-09.Growth plan: A plan for how the business will get bigger, for example by opening new locations or adding new products.
BMA-09.Sustainability plan: A plan that sets goals for reducing the harm the business does to the environment, such as cutting waste and energy use.
BMA-09.Compensation plan: A plan that sets out how employees will be paid, including wage levels, raises, bonuses and commissions.
BMA-09.Merchandise plan: A retailer's plan for what goods to stock, how much of each to buy and when, so that sales targets can be met.

BMA-10.Chain of command: The unbroken line of authority that runs from the top of an organization to the bottom and shows who reports to whom.
BMA-10.Delegation: A manager handing a task, and the authority needed to do it, to a subordinate. The manager still answers for the result.
BMA-10.Division of labor: Splitting work into separate, narrower jobs so that each worker becomes skilled and fast at one part. Also called specialization.
BMA-10.Span of control: The number of employees who report directly to one manager. A wide span means fewer managers and a flatter organization.
BMA-10.Authority: The right that comes with a position to make decisions, give orders and use resources.
BMA-10.Responsibility: The duty to carry out a task that has been assigned. A person who accepts a job takes on the obligation to do it.
BMA-10.Accountability: Having to answer to a superior for results. An employee who is given a task must report on and accept the outcome.
BMA-10.Departmentalization: Grouping jobs into units, for example by function, product, customer or region, so that related work is managed together.
BMA-10.Organizational chart: A diagram of the positions in a company and the lines of authority that connect them.
BMA-10.Centralization: Keeping the power to make decisions with a small number of managers at the top of the organization.
BMA-10.Decentralization: Pushing the power to make decisions down to lower-level managers and employees who are closer to the work.
BMA-10.Unity of command: The principle that each employee should report to only one boss, so that no one receives conflicting orders.
BMA-10.Empowerment: Giving front-line employees the authority to make decisions and solve problems without first asking a manager.
BMA-10.Coordination: Linking the work of different people and departments so that their efforts fit together toward the same goals.
BMA-10.Line and staff authority: Line managers have direct authority over the people who produce or sell. Staff specialists, such as legal or human resources, advise and support them.
BMA-10.Formalization: The degree to which jobs are governed by written rules and standard procedures instead of being left to the judgment of the worker.
BMA-10.Job design: Deciding which tasks, duties and responsibilities belong to each job and how the job relates to others.
BMA-10.Work teams: Small groups of employees who share responsibility for a result. Organizing by teams can replace some layers of supervision.
BMA-10.Levels of management: The layers of managers between the top and the bottom of an organization. Many layers make a tall structure and few make a flat one.
BMA-10.Unity of direction: The principle, from Henri Fayol, that all activities with the same objective should be guided by one manager using one plan.
BMA-10.Parity of authority and responsibility: The principle that a person given responsibility for a task must also be given enough authority to carry it out.
BMA-10.Exception principle: The idea that routine matters should be handled at lower levels and only unusual problems passed up to higher managers.
BMA-10.Informal organization: The network of friendships and unofficial contacts among employees, which exists alongside the formal structure and carries much communication.
BMA-10.Mechanistic and organic structures: Two opposite designs: a mechanistic organization is rigid, with strict rules and central control, and an organic one is flexible and decentralized.

ECO-08.Competition: Rivalry among sellers for the same customers. It pushes businesses to keep prices down and quality up.
ECO-08.Private property: The right of individuals and businesses, not the government, to own land, buildings, equipment and other resources and to use or sell them.
ECO-08.Profit motive: The desire to earn a profit, which is what drives people to start businesses, take risks and produce what buyers want.
ECO-08.Freedom of choice: Consumers are free to decide what to buy and from whom, and owners are free to decide how to use what they own.
ECO-08.Supply and demand: Prices are set by buyers and sellers in the market, not by the government, and those prices signal what should be produced.
ECO-08.Limited government: The government mostly stays out of business decisions. Its main jobs are to enforce laws and contracts and protect property rights.
ECO-08.Voluntary exchange: Buyers and sellers trade only when each chooses to, so a trade takes place only if both sides expect to be better off.
ECO-08.Freedom of enterprise: Anyone may start a business, choose what to produce and sell it in the market of their choice, within the law.
ECO-08.Self-interest: People act to benefit themselves: owners seek profit, workers seek higher pay and buyers seek the best deal. Competition steers this toward what others want.
ECO-08.Consumer sovereignty: The idea that consumers rule the market: what they choose to buy decides which goods are produced and which businesses survive.
ECO-08.Risk: The chance of losing money. In a market economy owners can earn profits, but nothing protects them from failing.
ECO-08.Freedom of contract: People and businesses are free to make legally binding agreements with one another on terms they choose.
ECO-08.Incentives: Rewards such as profit and higher wages that encourage people to work, save, invest and invent.
ECO-08.Specialization: People and businesses concentrate on what they do best and trade for the rest, which raises total output.
ECO-08.Freedom to choose an occupation: Workers may decide what kind of work to do and whom to work for, instead of being assigned a job.
ECO-08.Innovation: Competition and the chance of profit push businesses to keep developing new products and better ways of making them.
ECO-08.Wide variety of goods: Because many businesses compete to meet different wants, shoppers can choose from a large range of products and services.
ECO-08.Income inequality: Incomes depend on what each person can sell in the market, so some people earn far more than others. It is a common criticism of market economies.
ECO-08.Business cycles: Market economies tend to move through periods of growth followed by periods of decline, instead of growing at a steady rate.
ECO-08.Decentralized decision making: Millions of households and businesses each make their own choices about what to buy and produce. No central planner decides for them.
ECO-08.Use of money: Money is used for nearly all exchanges, which makes trading far easier than swapping one good directly for another.
ECO-08.Capital goods and technology: Market economies rely heavily on tools, machines and advanced technology, because competition rewards more efficient ways of producing.

ECO-09.Technology: New tools, machines and methods let the same workers and resources produce more. Economists see it as the main source of long-run growth.
ECO-09.Education: Schooling and training build human capital, the knowledge and skills of workers. Better-educated workers produce more and adopt new technology faster.
ECO-09.Natural resources: Land, minerals, energy, water and farmland that a country can use or sell. They help growth, though some resource-poor countries have grown rich without them.
ECO-09.Capital investment: Spending on factories, machines, computers and other capital goods. Workers with more and better equipment can produce more per hour.
ECO-09.Productivity growth: A rise in the output produced by each worker or each hour worked. It is the only way living standards can keep rising once most people already have jobs.
ECO-09.Labor force growth: More people working means more total output. It makes the whole economy bigger, although output per person rises only if productivity rises too.
ECO-09.Infrastructure: Shared systems such as roads, ports, power lines, water and internet service, which lower the cost of producing and moving goods for every business.
ECO-09.Entrepreneurship: People who take the risk of starting businesses bring new products and methods to market, create jobs and push older firms to improve.
ECO-09.International trade: Selling to and buying from other countries gives businesses bigger markets and lets a country concentrate on what it produces best.
ECO-09.Stable government: A government that is steady, peaceful and honest gives people the confidence to build businesses and invest for the future.
ECO-09.Property rights: Laws and courts that protect what people own and enforce contracts. People invest and build only when they expect to keep what they earn.
ECO-09.Saving: Money that households and businesses set aside instead of spending. Banks and markets lend it out, which pays for new investment in capital goods.
ECO-09.Research and development: Work by businesses, universities and governments to discover new knowledge and turn it into new products and processes.
ECO-09.Foreign investment: Money from other countries used to build factories and businesses. It adds capital and often brings new technology and management skills with it.
ECO-09.Competition: Rivalry among businesses pushes each to cut costs, improve products and adopt better methods, which raises productivity across the economy.
ECO-09.Stable prices: When prices rise slowly and predictably, people can plan, save and sign long-term contracts with confidence. High inflation discourages investment.
ECO-09.Financial system: Banks and financial markets that move savings to the businesses with the best uses for them, so that good ideas can get funded.
ECO-09.Healthy population: Workers who are healthy miss less work, learn more and stay productive for more years, so good health adds to human capital.
ECO-09.Specialization: People, firms and regions concentrating on what they do best and trading for the rest, which raises the total amount produced.
ECO-09.Economic incentives: Rewards such as profit and higher pay that make it worthwhile to work, save, invest and invent. Growth slows when effort and risk go unrewarded.
ECO-09.Large market: Many customers let businesses produce in large volumes at a lower cost per unit, and make it worth paying for costly research and equipment.
ECO-09.Technology transfer: Adopting methods already invented elsewhere. A poorer country can grow quickly by copying proven technology instead of inventing its own.
ECO-09.Intellectual property protection: Patents and copyrights that give inventors and creators the sole right to profit from their work for a time, which encourages research and invention.

ECO-10.Consumer good: A product bought by households for their own use, such as food, clothing or a phone.
ECO-10.Capital good: A product that businesses buy to help make other goods and services, such as machinery, tools or a delivery truck.
ECO-10.Substitute good: A good that can be used in place of another, such as tea for coffee. When the price of one rises, demand for the other goes up.
ECO-10.Complementary good: A good that is used together with another, such as printers and ink. When the price of one rises, demand for the other falls.
ECO-10.Luxury good: A good that people want but can do without, such as jewelry. Demand for it rises faster than income does.
ECO-10.Necessity: A good that people need and keep buying even when prices rise or incomes fall, such as basic food or electricity.
ECO-10.Public good: A good that everyone can use at once and no one can be kept from using, such as national defense, so it is usually paid for with taxes.
ECO-10.Private good: A good that only the buyer gets to use, and that is used up when consumed, such as a sandwich. Most goods sold in stores are private goods.
ECO-10.Durable good: A good that lasts and is used for a long time, usually three years or more, such as a car, furniture or a refrigerator.
ECO-10.Nondurable good: A good that is used up quickly or lasts only a short time, such as food, gasoline or paper products.
ECO-10.Normal good: A good that people buy more of when their incomes rise and less of when their incomes fall.
ECO-10.Inferior good: A good that people buy less of when their incomes rise, because they switch to something they like better, such as from instant noodles to fresh food.
ECO-10.Intermediate good: A good that is used up in making another product, such as the flour a bakery buys or the tires a carmaker installs.
ECO-10.Final good: A finished good sold to the person or business that will actually use it, not one resold or made into something else.
ECO-10.Free good: A good that is so plentiful that it has no price and no one has to give anything up to get it, such as air.
ECO-10.Economic good: A good that is scarce, so getting it means paying a price or giving something else up. Nearly everything sold is an economic good.
ECO-10.Giffen good: A rare kind of inferior good, usually a basic food, that poor households buy more of when its price rises because they can no longer afford better food.
ECO-10.Veblen good: A luxury good that people want more as its price rises, because the high price itself is a sign of status.
ECO-10.Merit good: A good that society judges people should have whether or not they can pay, such as schooling or vaccines, so governments often provide or subsidize it.
ECO-10.Common resource: A good that no one can be kept from using but that one person's use leaves less of for others, such as fish in the ocean.
ECO-10.Commodity: A basic good, such as wheat, oil or copper, that is the same no matter who produces it and is traded in bulk.
ECO-10.Club good: A good that people can be kept from using unless they pay, but that many can use at once without using it up, such as streaming television.
ECO-10.Demerit good: A good that society judges to be harmful to the people who use it, such as tobacco, so governments often tax or restrict it.
ECO-10.Experience good: A good whose quality a buyer can judge only after using it, such as a restaurant meal or a haircut.
ECO-10.Search good: A good whose quality a buyer can check before buying, such as a piece of clothing or furniture.
ECO-10.Credence good: A good whose quality is hard for a buyer to judge even after using it, such as a car repair or a vitamin supplement.

HRM-07.Recruiting: Finding and attracting people to apply for open jobs, for example through job postings, career fairs and referrals.
HRM-07.Training: Teaching employees the knowledge and skills they need for their current jobs and preparing them for future ones.
HRM-07.Compensation: Deciding how much each job pays and making sure that wages and salaries are fair, competitive and paid correctly.
HRM-07.Benefits administration: Choosing and running the benefit programs a company offers, such as health insurance, retirement plans and paid time off.
HRM-07.Performance management: Setting up the system by which managers set goals, review how well each employee is doing and give feedback.
HRM-07.Selection: Choosing the best applicant for a job through steps such as screening applications, interviewing and checking references.
HRM-07.Onboarding: Helping new hires settle in by completing their paperwork and introducing them to the company, its rules and their coworkers.
HRM-07.Employee relations: Keeping a good relationship between the company and its workers, including handling complaints and settling conflicts fairly.
HRM-07.Termination: Managing how employees leave the company, whether they quit, retire, are laid off or are fired, including the final paperwork.
HRM-07.Legal compliance: Making sure the company follows employment laws on matters such as discrimination, wages, hours and leave.
HRM-07.Health and safety: Working to keep the workplace free of hazards, training employees in safe practices and recording any injuries.
HRM-07.Policy development: Writing and updating the rules of the workplace, such as attendance and dress policies, and publishing them in an employee handbook.
HRM-07.Record keeping: Maintaining accurate and confidential files on every employee, including pay, benefits, reviews and legally required forms.
HRM-07.Discipline: Setting up and applying a fair process for dealing with employees who break the rules or perform poorly.
HRM-07.Human resource planning: Forecasting how many employees with which skills the company will need in the future and planning how to have them in place.
HRM-07.Job analysis: Studying a job to identify its duties and the skills it requires. The result is used to write the job description.
HRM-07.Labor relations: Dealing with labor unions on behalf of the company, including negotiating and applying the union contract.
HRM-07.Employee retention: Working to keep good employees from leaving, for example by improving pay, career paths and working conditions.
HRM-07.Employee engagement: Measuring and improving how satisfied and committed employees feel, for example through surveys and recognition programs.
HRM-07.Promotions and transfers: Managing the movement of employees into higher-level jobs or into other departments and locations within the company.
HRM-07.Career development: Helping employees plan and grow their careers inside the company, for example through career paths, mentoring and leadership programs.
HRM-07.Succession planning: Identifying and developing employees who can step into key positions when the people now holding them leave.
HRM-07.Diversity and inclusion: Working to build a workforce of people from different backgrounds and a workplace where all of them are treated fairly and feel welcome.
HRM-07.Employee wellness: Offering programs that support the physical and mental health of employees, such as counseling services and fitness programs.
HRM-07.HR information systems: Running the software that stores employee data and handles tasks such as payroll, benefits enrollment and time tracking.
HRM-07.Organizational development: Helping the company plan and carry out major changes, such as a restructuring, in a way employees can adapt to.

HRM-08.Full-time: Working the employer's standard full week, commonly around 40 hours, usually with access to the full range of company benefits.
HRM-08.Part-time: Working fewer hours each week than the employer's full-time standard, often with fewer benefits.
HRM-08.Remote work: Doing the job from home or another place outside the employer's office, using a computer and the internet to stay connected.
HRM-08.Flextime: A schedule that lets employees choose when they start and finish, as long as they work the required hours and are present during set core times.
HRM-08.Temporary work: A job that lasts for a limited time, such as covering a busy period or an absent employee, often arranged through a staffing agency.
HRM-08.Hybrid work: An arrangement in which employees split their time between working at the office and working remotely.
HRM-08.Seasonal work: A job that exists only during a certain part of the year, such as retail work in the holiday season or lifeguarding in summer.
HRM-08.Shift work: A schedule in which different groups of employees work at different times, such as day, evening and night, so the business can run for longer hours.
HRM-08.Independent contractor: A self-employed person hired to do a particular job or project. The person is not an employee, so receives no benefits and handles their own taxes.
HRM-08.Internship: A short-term position, paid or unpaid, that gives a student or beginner work experience in a career field.
HRM-08.Compressed workweek: Working the full weekly hours in fewer days, for example four ten-hour days instead of five eight-hour days.
HRM-08.Job sharing: An arrangement in which two part-time employees split the duties, hours and pay of one full-time job.
HRM-08.On-call work: An arrangement in which a worker has no fixed hours and comes in only when the employer needs them.
HRM-08.Apprenticeship: A paid arrangement that combines work under a skilled worker with classroom instruction, leading to a recognized qualification in a trade.
HRM-08.Split shift: A workday divided into two or more parts with a long unpaid break between them, common in restaurants and transit.
HRM-08.Staggered hours: Employees work fixed schedules that start and end at different times from one another, which eases crowding and extends coverage.
HRM-08.Phased retirement: An arrangement that lets an older employee cut back hours gradually over time instead of stopping work all at once.
HRM-08.Employee leasing: An arrangement in which an outside firm is the legal employer of the workers and handles their payroll and benefits, while they work at the client business.
HRM-08.Fixed-term contract: Employment that is agreed to last for a set period or until a project ends, after which it stops unless renewed.
HRM-08.At-will employment: The usual arrangement in the United States, in which either the employer or the employee may end the job at any time for any lawful reason.
HRM-08.Probationary employment: A trial period at the start of a job during which the employer judges whether the new hire is a good fit before the hire becomes regular.
HRM-08.Temp-to-hire: An arrangement in which a worker starts as a temporary and may be offered a regular job if the trial period goes well.
HRM-08.Results-only work environment: An arrangement in which employees are judged only on what they produce and are free to decide when and where they work.
HRM-08.Annualized hours: A contract for a set number of hours over the whole year, worked in longer weeks at busy times and shorter weeks at quiet times.

HRM-09.Low pay: Wages or a salary below what the employee needs or could earn for the same work at another company.
HRM-09.Poor management: A supervisor who treats people badly, gives little support or direction, or controls every detail of the work.
HRM-09.Better job offer: Another employer offers a job the employee finds more attractive, for example because of the pay, the role or the location.
HRM-09.Lack of advancement: The employee sees no chance of being promoted or of growing in the job, so looks for a career path somewhere else.
HRM-09.Burnout: Physical and mental exhaustion caused by long hours, heavy workloads or constant stress over a long period.
HRM-09.Poor work-life balance: The job leaves too little time or flexibility for family, rest and personal life.
HRM-09.Toxic workplace culture: A work environment marked by disrespect, bullying, harassment or unsafe conditions, which makes people dread coming to work.
HRM-09.Lack of recognition: Employees feel that their effort and results go unnoticed and that the company does not value them.
HRM-09.Retirement: The employee stops working altogether, usually on reaching an age or level of savings that makes it possible.
HRM-09.Layoff: The employer ends the job because of a lack of work or money, not because of anything the employee did.
HRM-09.Fired: The employer ends the job because of poor performance or misconduct. This is involuntary turnover.
HRM-09.Relocation: The employee moves to another area, often for family reasons or a partner's job, and can no longer get to the workplace.
HRM-09.Poor benefits: The company offers little or no health insurance, retirement plan or paid time off compared with other employers.
HRM-09.Boredom: The work is repetitive or too easy, so the employee loses interest and satisfaction in the job.
HRM-09.Conflict with coworkers: Ongoing disagreements or bad relationships with other employees that make the workplace unpleasant.
HRM-09.Family reasons: Responsibilities at home, such as caring for a child or a sick relative, that make it hard to keep the job.
HRM-09.Long commute: The time, cost or difficulty of traveling to and from the workplace becomes more than the employee is willing to accept.
HRM-09.Lack of training: Employees are not given the instruction they need to do the job well or to build new skills, so they become frustrated and leave.
HRM-09.Poor job fit: The job turns out not to match the skills, interests or expectations of the person hired, often because of a rushed hiring decision.
HRM-09.Returning to school: The employee leaves to study full time, such as a student going off to college at the end of summer.
HRM-09.Health problems: An illness, injury or disability makes the employee unable to continue in the job.
HRM-09.Career change: The employee decides to move into a different line of work or to start a business of their own.
HRM-09.Job insecurity: Employees who fear the company is in trouble or that layoffs are coming often leave first for a safer job.
HRM-09.Lack of autonomy: Employees have no say in how they do their work or in decisions that affect them, and feel they are not trusted.
HRM-09.Unfair treatment: Employees believe that pay, promotions or discipline are handed out unequally, for example through favoritism or discrimination.
HRM-09.End of contract: A temporary, seasonal or fixed-term job reaches its planned end date and the worker is not kept on.
HRM-09.Merger or reorganization: A major change in ownership or structure brings new bosses, roles and uncertainty, which leads some employees to leave.
HRM-09.Disagreement with company values: The employee no longer agrees with the direction, ethics or behavior of the company or its leaders.

OPM-07.Gloves: Hand coverings chosen for the hazard, such as rubber gloves for chemicals, cut-resistant gloves for blades or disposable gloves for food and medical work.
OPM-07.Safety glasses: Impact-resistant eyewear that protects the eyes from flying particles, dust and splashes. Goggles seal more closely around the eyes.
OPM-07.Hard hat: A rigid helmet that protects the head from falling objects and bumps, required on construction sites and in many factories.
OPM-07.Face mask: A covering over the nose and mouth that limits the dust or germs a worker breathes in or spreads to others.
OPM-07.Steel-toe boots: Work boots with a reinforced toe cap that protects the feet from heavy falling or rolling objects.
OPM-07.Earplugs: Small inserts worn in the ears to reduce loud noise and prevent hearing loss. Earmuffs do the same job from outside the ear.
OPM-07.High-visibility vest: A brightly colored vest with reflective strips that makes a worker easy to see near traffic or moving equipment.
OPM-07.Respirator: A tight-fitting device worn over the nose and mouth that filters harmful dust, fumes or gases out of the air or supplies clean air.
OPM-07.Face shield: A clear panel that covers the whole face to protect it from splashes, sparks and flying debris.
OPM-07.Apron: A covering for the front of the body that protects against spills, heat, cuts or, in a lead-lined version, X-rays.
OPM-07.Safety harness: A set of straps worn around the body and attached to an anchor point to stop a fall when working at height.
OPM-07.Coveralls: A one-piece garment worn over regular clothes to keep chemicals, dirt or other hazards off the body.
OPM-07.Lab coat: A knee-length coat worn in laboratories and medical settings to keep spills and contamination off the skin and clothing.
OPM-07.Welding helmet: A helmet with a dark filter lens that protects a welder's eyes and face from intense light, sparks and heat.
OPM-07.Knee pads: Cushioned guards strapped over the knees to protect workers who kneel a lot, such as flooring installers.
OPM-07.Life jacket: A buoyant vest that keeps a person afloat, worn by people who work on or near water.
OPM-07.Shoe covers: Disposable coverings pulled over shoes to keep dirt and germs out of a clean area or to keep the shoes from being contaminated.
OPM-07.Rubber boots: Waterproof boots that keep the feet dry and protect them from chemicals, mud or wet floors.
OPM-07.Flame-resistant clothing: Garments made of material that resists catching fire, worn by firefighters, electricians and workers near open flames.
OPM-07.Chainsaw chaps: Leg coverings made with fibers that jam a chainsaw's chain on contact, worn by loggers and tree workers.
OPM-07.Bump cap: A lightweight cap with a thin shell that protects the head from minor bumps in tight spaces. It is not built to stop falling objects.
OPM-07.Protective sleeves: Coverings worn over the arms to guard against cuts, heat or chemical splashes.
OPM-07.Metatarsal guards: Shields that cover the top of the foot, behind the toes, to protect it from heavy objects that are dropped.
OPM-07.Body armor: A protective vest that resists bullets or blades, worn by police officers and security guards.

OPM-08.Identify the need: The first step: someone in the business recognizes that a good or service is required, such as stock running low or a machine wearing out.
OPM-08.Place the order: Sending the chosen supplier a purchase order that states exactly what is wanted, how many, at what price and when it must arrive.
OPM-08.Select a supplier: Choosing which vendor to buy from after weighing price, quality, delivery time, service and reliability.
OPM-08.Receive the goods: Accepting the delivery when it arrives and counting it against the order and the packing slip.
OPM-08.Pay the invoice: Paying the supplier's bill by the due date, once the business has confirmed that it received what it ordered.
OPM-08.Compare prices: Asking several suppliers for quotes or bids on the same item and comparing their prices and terms.
OPM-08.Find suppliers: Searching for vendors that are able to provide the item, for example through catalogs, trade shows, websites and referrals.
OPM-08.Inspect the goods: Checking the delivered items for damage and for the right quality and type before accepting them.
OPM-08.Negotiate terms: Discussing price, discounts, delivery dates and payment terms with a supplier to reach the best deal for the business.
OPM-08.Write specifications: Describing exactly what is needed, such as size, quality, material and performance, so suppliers can quote on the right item.
OPM-08.Purchase requisition: An internal form in which a department asks the purchasing department to buy something. It is a request, not yet an order.
OPM-08.Get approval: Having a manager with the proper authority sign off on the purchase before any money is committed.
OPM-08.Follow up on the order: Checking with the supplier after ordering to make sure the shipment is on schedule, and pressing for delivery if it is late.
OPM-08.Determine quantity: Working out how much to order, by weighing how fast the item is used against the cost of storing extra stock.
OPM-08.Match invoice to order: Comparing the supplier's bill with the purchase order and the receiving record, so the business pays only for what it ordered and got.
OPM-08.Keep records: Filing the documents for each purchase and updating inventory and accounting records, so there is a trail to check later.
OPM-08.Evaluate supplier performance: Reviewing after the purchase how well the vendor did on quality, price and on-time delivery, to decide whether to use it again.
OPM-08.Store the goods: Moving the received items into the stockroom or warehouse and adding them to inventory so they are ready for use or sale.
OPM-08.Check the budget: Confirming that money has been set aside for the purchase and that the cost fits within the spending limit.
OPM-08.Return defective goods: Sending back items that arrive damaged, wrong or below standard and getting a replacement or a credit from the supplier.
OPM-08.Award the contract: Formally giving the business to the winning bidder and signing an agreement that sets out the terms of supply.
OPM-08.Make-or-buy decision: Deciding early in the process whether the business should produce an item itself or purchase it from an outside supplier.
OPM-08.Prepare a receiving report: Writing up what was actually delivered, how many and in what condition, as the official record of receipt.

OPM-09.Productivity: The amount of output produced for each unit of input, most often measured as output per worker or per hour of labor.
OPM-09.Defect rate: The share of units produced that fail to meet the quality standard. A lower rate means better quality.
OPM-09.Output: The total number of units a process produces in a given period, such as cars built per week.
OPM-09.Unit cost: The total cost of production divided by the number of units made, which shows what each unit costs to produce.
OPM-09.On-time delivery: The percentage of orders that reach the customer by the promised date.
OPM-09.Downtime: The time that equipment or a production line is stopped when it should be running, for example because of a breakdown. Uptime, its opposite, is the share of time it is available.
OPM-09.Lead time: The total time from when an order is placed until the finished product is delivered to the customer.
OPM-09.Capacity utilization: The share of the maximum possible output that a plant or machine is actually producing.
OPM-09.Cycle time: The time it takes to complete one unit, or one full run of a process, from start to finish.
OPM-09.Inventory turnover: The number of times in a period that inventory is sold or used up and replaced. Faster turnover means less money tied up in stock.
OPM-09.Throughput: The rate at which a process turns out finished units, such as 200 units an hour.
OPM-09.Scrap rate: The share of materials or units that must be thrown away because they are faulty and cannot be repaired.
OPM-09.Customer satisfaction: How well the product and service meet customer expectations, measured through surveys, complaints and returns.
OPM-09.Safety incident rate: The number of workplace injuries and accidents compared with the hours worked. It shows how safely the operation runs.
OPM-09.Order accuracy: The percentage of orders shipped with exactly the right items in the right quantities.
OPM-09.Fill rate: The percentage of customer demand that is met right away from stock on hand, without a delay or a back order.
OPM-09.Yield: The share of the units started that come out as good finished products. First-pass yield counts only those right the first time, with no rework.
OPM-09.Overall equipment effectiveness: A combined score for a machine or line that multiplies its availability, its speed and the quality of what it makes.
OPM-09.Takt time: The pace at which one unit must be finished to keep up with customer demand: the working time available divided by the units demanded.
OPM-09.Labor hours per unit: The amount of worker time needed to make one unit of a product. Fewer hours per unit means higher labor efficiency.
OPM-09.Backlog: The orders that have been received but not yet filled. A growing backlog shows that demand is outrunning production.
OPM-09.Schedule attainment: The share of the planned production that was actually completed in the period, which shows how well the plant keeps to its schedule.
OPM-09.Changeover time: The time needed to switch a machine or line from making one product to making another.
OPM-09.Work in process: The amount of partly finished product sitting in the production system. A high level can signal a bottleneck.
OPM-09.Mean time between failures: The average length of time a piece of equipment runs before it breaks down, a measure of its reliability.
OPM-09.Cost of quality: The total money spent on preventing defects, checking for them and fixing the failures that still occur.
OPM-09.Process capability: A statistical measure of how consistently a process can produce output that falls within the specification limits.

POB-08.Communication: The ability to speak and write clearly so that coworkers, managers and customers understand you.
POB-08.Teamwork: The ability to work well with other people toward a shared goal, doing your part and helping others do theirs.
POB-08.Work ethic: A belief in working hard and doing the job properly, even when no one is watching.
POB-08.Problem solving: The ability to work out what is causing a difficulty and find a practical way to fix it.
POB-08.Time management: Planning and using your working time well, so that tasks are finished by their deadlines and the most important come first.
POB-08.Dependability: Being someone others can count on: showing up on time, every time, and doing what you said you would do.
POB-08.Leadership: The ability to guide and motivate other people and to take charge when a situation calls for it.
POB-08.Critical thinking: Looking at information carefully and logically before reaching a conclusion or making a decision.
POB-08.Adaptability: The ability to adjust calmly to new tasks, tools, schedules and situations instead of resisting change.
