POB-08.Positive attitude: Approaching work and coworkers with energy and optimism, including on difficult days.
POB-08.Honesty: Telling the truth and doing the right thing, so that the employer and customers can trust you with money, property and information.
POB-08.Computer skills: The ability to use common technology at work, such as email, word processing, spreadsheets and online tools.
POB-08.Interpersonal skills: The ability to get along with many kinds of people and to understand how they feel. Often called people skills.
POB-08.Initiative: Seeing what needs to be done and doing it without being told.
POB-08.Organization: Keeping your work, materials and schedule in order so that nothing is lost or forgotten.
POB-08.Creativity: The ability to come up with new ideas and fresh ways of doing things.
POB-08.Willingness to learn: Being open to instruction and feedback and eager to pick up new skills as the job changes.
POB-08.Listening: Paying full attention to what others say so that you understand instructions and customer needs correctly.
POB-08.Professionalism: Behaving, dressing and speaking in a way that suits the workplace and shows respect for others.
POB-08.Attention to detail: Working carefully and checking your work so that small mistakes do not slip through.
POB-08.Customer service: The ability to treat customers politely and helpfully so that they are satisfied and want to return.
POB-08.Basic reading and math skills: The ability to read instructions and documents and to do everyday calculations, such as making change or measuring.
POB-08.Conflict resolution: The ability to settle disagreements with coworkers or customers calmly and fairly.
POB-08.Self-management: Controlling your own emotions and behavior and staying on task without needing constant supervision.
POB-08.Cultural awareness: Understanding and respecting that people have different backgrounds and customs, and working well with all of them.
POB-08.Accountability: Accepting responsibility for your own work and actions, including admitting and fixing your mistakes.
POB-08.Multitasking: The ability to keep track of several tasks or demands in the same period and move between them without dropping any.

POB-09.Profit: Earning more in revenue than the business spends in costs. It rewards the owners and pays for future growth.
POB-09.Growth: Becoming a bigger business, for example by opening new locations, entering new markets or adding products.
POB-09.Increase sales: Raising the amount of goods or services sold, often stated as a target such as a certain percentage more than last year.
POB-09.Customer satisfaction: Meeting or exceeding what customers expect, so that they return, spend more and recommend the business to others.
POB-09.Market share: Winning a larger percentage of the total sales in a market compared with competitors.
POB-09.Survival: Simply staying in business by covering costs. It is the main goal of many new businesses and of any business in a downturn.
POB-09.Social responsibility: Acting in ways that benefit society and the community, not only the owners, such as supporting local causes and behaving ethically.
POB-09.Product quality: Making goods or delivering services that reliably meet a high standard, with few defects or complaints.
POB-09.Reduce costs: Lowering what it costs to run the business or make each product, which raises profit without raising prices.
POB-09.Gain new customers: Bringing in buyers who have not purchased from the business before, which widens its customer base.
POB-09.Employee satisfaction: Being a good place to work, so that employees are motivated, productive and less likely to leave.
POB-09.Innovation: Developing new or improved products, services or methods so the business stays ahead of changing customer wants.
POB-09.Brand recognition: Making the name and image of the business well known and well regarded among its target customers.
POB-09.Sustainability: Operating in a way that limits harm to the environment, for example by cutting waste, energy use and emissions.
POB-09.Efficiency: Getting more output from the same resources, or the same output from fewer, by wasting less time, labor and material.
POB-09.Shareholder value: Increasing the wealth of the owners of a corporation through a rising share price and dividends.
POB-09.Financial stability: Keeping enough cash coming in and debt low enough that the business can always pay its bills and get through hard times.
POB-09.Competitive advantage: Building something that sets the business apart from rivals and is hard for them to copy, such as lower costs or better service.
POB-09.Diversification: Spreading into different products or markets so the business does not depend on a single source of income.
POB-09.Workplace safety: Running the business so that employees are not injured, often expressed as a target such as zero accidents.
POB-09.Owner independence: Keeping control in the hands of the owner or family. Some owners turn down growth or outside investors to stay their own boss.
POB-09.Going public or being acquired: Building the business to the point where its owners can sell shares on a stock exchange or sell the whole company to a larger firm.
POB-09.Fulfill a social mission: Solving a social or environmental problem as the main purpose of the business, with profit as the means of paying for it.
POB-09.Legal compliance: Following all the laws and regulations that apply to the business, so that it avoids fines, lawsuits and damage to its name.
POB-09.Workforce diversity: Employing people from a wide range of backgrounds and making sure all of them have a fair chance to succeed.

POB-10.Limited liability: The owners can lose only the money they invested. Their homes, savings and other personal property cannot be taken to pay the debts of the corporation.
POB-10.Owned by stockholders: Ownership is divided into shares of stock. Each person who holds shares owns a part of the corporation, and a large one can have many thousands of owners.
POB-10.Separate legal entity: The law treats a corporation as a person in its own right, apart from the people who own it. This is the feature that most of the others follow from.
POB-10.Easier to raise capital: A corporation can bring in large sums by selling shares of stock to investors or by issuing bonds, which the other forms of ownership cannot do.
POB-10.Board of directors: A group elected by the stockholders to oversee the corporation. The board sets major policy and hires the top officers.
POB-10.Double taxation: A corporation pays income tax on its profits, and stockholders then pay tax again on the dividends they receive from those same profits.
POB-10.Unlimited life: A corporation keeps existing when an owner dies or sells out. A sole proprietorship ends with its owner, and a partnership can end when a partner leaves.
POB-10.Easy transfer of ownership: An owner can leave simply by selling shares to someone else, without the consent of the other owners and without disturbing the business.
POB-10.Separation of ownership and management: The stockholders own the corporation but usually do not run it. Hired professional managers make the day-to-day decisions.
POB-10.Created by a state charter: A corporation comes into existence only when a state approves its articles of incorporation. A sole proprietorship or general partnership needs no such approval.
POB-10.More government regulation: Corporations must follow more rules and file more reports with state and federal agencies than the other forms of ownership.
POB-10.Costly and complex to form: Setting up a corporation takes legal paperwork and filing fees, and usually a lawyer, which makes it the hardest form of ownership to start.
POB-10.Dividends: Profits reach the owners as dividends, payments per share that the board of directors chooses to declare. Owners cannot simply take money out of the business.
POB-10.Corporate officers: Top managers, such as the chief executive officer, who are appointed by the board of directors to run the corporation day to day.
POB-10.Bylaws: The written rules a corporation adopts for governing itself, covering matters such as how directors are elected and when meetings are held.
POB-10.Stockholder voting rights: Owners of common stock vote, usually one vote per share, to elect the directors and decide major questions, often at an annual meeting.
POB-10.Can sue and be sued: As a legal person, a corporation can own property, sign contracts and go to court in its own name instead of in the names of its owners.
POB-10.Public financial disclosure: A corporation whose stock is sold to the public must publish its financial results, so competitors and anyone else can read them.
POB-10.Agency problem: The risk that hired managers will act in their own interest instead of in the interest of the stockholders who own the company.
POB-10.Required formalities: A corporation must hold regular meetings of directors and stockholders and keep written minutes, or risk losing the legal protection its owners enjoy.
POB-10.Stock can be publicly traded: A corporation can offer its shares to the general public and have them bought and sold on a stock exchange. No other form of ownership can.
